nodes.title: Roth's theorem
nodes.statement: Let α be a real algebraic number of degree ≥ 2 (equivalently, algebraic and irrational) and κ > 2 (κ = 2 + ε, ε > 0). Then only finitely many rational numbers ξ satisfy |α − ξ| ≤ H(ξ)^{-κ}, where H(x/y) = max(|x|, |y|) for coprime x, y (Mathlib's mulHeight₁). The proof shows finiteness only: it provides no bound for the heights of the solutions and no way to list them.
hypotheses: α ∈ ℝ algebraic over ℚ and irrational
proofSteps: Suppose the solution set S is infinite. Fix ε ∈ (0, 1/12) with κ(1/2 − 3ε) > 1, then n ≥ 1 with e^{ε^2 n/4} ≥ 2d, σ = (5ε/4)^{2^{n−1}}, M = 2σ^{-1}, C_1 := max(log C, log 2) with C from roth-auxiliary-polynomial, C_2 := 4C_1 + 2 log 2 + 2 log max(1, |α|), and L ≥ σ^{-1}((5/2)C_1 + 5n) so large that 1 + C_2/(nL) < κ(1/2 − 3ε) (parameters depend only on α and κ; L is fixed before the β_i).
rapidly-increasing-good-approximations gives β_1..β_n ∈ S with h(β_1) ≥ L, h(β_{i+1}) ≥ M h(β_i).

For each integer D ≥ 5h(β_n) put r_i = ⌊D/h(β_i)⌋ (roth-weights-satisfy-roth-lemma-hypotheses) and take P from roth-auxiliary-polynomial; by height-of-integer-polynomial-bound, h(P) ≤ C_1 ∑ r_i, so roth-lemma over K = ℚ gives Ind_{β,r}(P) ≤ 2nσ^{1/2^{n−1}} = (5/2)nε.
roth-nonvanishing-derivative gives Q with Ind_α(Q) ≥ (1/2 − 3ε)n, Q(β) ≠ 0 and log|coeff Q| ≤ 4C_1 D/L.

roth-denominator-lower-bound and roth-archimedean-upper-bound (t = (1/2 − 3ε)n, D' = D − h(β_n) ≤ r_i h(β_i)) give κ(D − h(β_n))(1/2 − 3ε)n ≤ ∑ r_i log den(β_i) + 4C_1 D/L + (2D/L)(log 2 + log max(1, |α|)) + 2n log(D + 1) ≤ nD + C_2 D/L + 2n log(D + 1), using log den(β_i) ≤ h(β_i) and r_i h(β_i) ≤ D.
Divide by nD and let D → ∞ with the β_i fixed: κ(1/2 − 3ε) ≤ 1 + C_2/(nL), contradicting the choice of L.
acceptance: Exponent comparison: Liouville gives κ = d, Thue κ > d/2 + 1, Roth κ > 2; the exponent 2 is optimal by Dirichlet's theorem (Evertse, p. 109).
Concrete instance (Evertse, Exercise 6.5): lacunary-series-transcendental.
Ineffectivity: the argument needs n good approximations of rapidly increasing heights and gives no bound on their heights (Evertse, p. 110).
Evertse, Corollary 7.2 deduces the same statement from the Subspace Theorem (stage DT.2); the proof planned here does not use the Subspace Theorem.

nodes.title: Roth's theorem as a lower bound (Evertse, Theorem 6.2)
nodes.statement: Let α be a real algebraic irrational number and κ > 2. There is c(α, κ) > 0 with |ξ − α| ≥ c(α, κ) H(ξ)^{-κ} for every ξ ∈ ℚ. The constant is not effectively computable by the method.

proofSteps: By roth-theorem the set F of ξ with |ξ − α| ≤ H(ξ)^{-κ} is finite; each ξ ∈ F has |ξ − α| > 0 (α irrational).
Take c = min(1, min_{ξ ∈ F} |ξ − α| H(ξ)^{κ}) (Evertse, Exercise 6.1, (ii) ⇒ (i)).

nodes.title: Roth's theorem in the vocabulary of LiouvilleWith
nodes.statement: For every real algebraic α and every p > 2, α is not LiouvilleWith p (Mathlib's predicate: there is no C such that infinitely many n admit m with α ≠ m/n and |α − m/n| < C n^{-p}). Equivalently, the irrationality exponent of a real algebraic number is at most 2.
hypotheses: α ∈ ℝ algebraic
proofSteps: If α ∈ ℚ, LiouvilleWith p α fails since LiouvilleWith with p > 1 forces irrationality (LiouvilleWith.irrational).

If α is irrational and LiouvilleWith p α held, choose 2 < κ < p. The fractions m/n provided for infinitely many n take infinitely many distinct values (a single value ξ_0 ≠ α cannot satisfy |α − ξ_0| < C n^{-p} for infinitely many n). Each satisfies H(m/n) ≤ max(|m|, n) ≤ (|α| + 1)n for n large, hence |α − m/n| < C(|α| + 1)^p H(m/n)^{-p} ≤ H(m/n)^{-κ} once H(m/n) is large; by Northcott only finitely many of these values have small height, so infinitely many rationals satisfy |α − ξ| ≤ H(ξ)^{-κ}, contradicting roth-theorem.
acceptance: Mathlib's docstring for LiouvilleWith names this consequence of the Thue-Siegel-Roth theorem as not yet formalised.
Together with Dirichlet's theorem (DT.0) this says the irrationality exponent of a real algebraic irrational number is exactly 2.

sources.locator: Chapter 6, Exercise 6.1 and the discussion before Theorem 6.2, printed pp. 109-110

nodes.title: Transcendence of ∑ b^{-3^k} (Evertse, Exercise 6.5)
nodes.statement: For every integer b ≥ 2 the real number ∑_{k ≥ 1} b^{-3^k} is transcendental.
proofSteps: Let α be the sum and ξ_N = ∑_{k=1}^{N} b^{-3^k} = a_N/b^{3^N}, so H(ξ_N) ≤ b^{3^N} and 0 < α − ξ_N ≤ 2 b^{-3^{N+1}} = 2 (b^{3^N})^{-3} ≤ 2 H(ξ_N)^{-3}; the ξ_N are distinct.
If α were rational, liouville-inequality-with-explicit-constant (d = 1) would give |α − ξ_N| ≥ c H(ξ_N)^{-1}, false for large N.
If α were algebraic irrational, then with κ = 5/2 all but finitely many ξ_N satisfy |α − ξ_N| ≤ H(ξ_N)^{-5/2} (as 2H^{-3} ≤ H^{-5/2} for H ≥ 4), contradicting roth-theorem.
acceptance: The partial sums give an error bounded by a constant times H⁻³ and hence violate Roth at κ=5/2 if the sum is algebraic irrational. This bounded-exponent estimate alone does not establish the arbitrarily large exponents required by the Liouville-number criterion; no exact irrationality exponent is asserted here.

nodes.title: Factorisation of a square-free binary form over ℂ
nodes.statement: Let F ∈ ℂ[X, Y] be a nonzero binary form of degree d, not divisible by (aX + bY)^2 for any (a, b) ≠ (0, 0), and not divisible by Y. Then F = a_0 ∏_{i=1}^{d} (X − α_i Y) with a_0 ≠ 0 and α_1, ..., α_d pairwise distinct.
hypotheses: F homogeneous of degree d (Mathlib's IsHomogeneous)
the source's square-free condition
Y ∤ F
proofSteps: Y ∤ F means a_0 := F(1, 0) ≠ 0, so F(X, 1) has degree d and splits over ℂ: F(X, 1) = a_0 ∏ (X − α_i) (Polynomial.C_leadingCoeff_mul_prod_multiset_X_sub_C, IsAlgClosed.card_roots_eq_natDegree).
Both F and a_0 ∏(X − α_i Y) are forms of degree d with the same dehomogenization, hence equal (compare coefficients of X^k Y^{d−k}; Polynomial.homogenize).
If α_i = α_j for i ≠ j then (X − α_i Y)^2 | F, contrary to the hypothesis.
acceptance: F = X^2 Y − Y^3 is divisible by Y and excluded; F = X^3 − 2Y^3 factors with the three cube roots of 2.

nodes.title: Values of square-free binary forms (Evertse, Theorem 6.3)
nodes.statement: Let F ∈ ℤ[X, Y] be a square-free binary form of degree d ≥ 3 and κ > 2. There is c(F, κ) > 0 such that |F(x, y)| ≥ c(F, κ) max(|x|, |y|)^{d−κ} for all (x, y) ∈ ℤ^2 with F(x, y) ≠ 0.
hypotheses: F homogeneous of degree d ≥ 3 with integer coefficients
square-free in the source's sense (no square of a nonzero linear form divides F in ℂ[X, Y])
proofSteps: By symmetry (F(Y, X) is again square-free) it suffices to treat |y| ≥ |x|, so y ≠ 0 whenever F(x, y) ≠ 0.

If Y | F, write F = Y F₁ with F₁ square-free of degree d−1 and Y ∤ F₁. Apply the following root-factorisation argument directly to F₁, which works in every positive degree, then multiply its bound by |y| = max(|x|,|y|). This does not invoke the present d≥3 theorem recursively at degree 2. Otherwise apply that argument directly to F.
squarefree-binary-form-factorisation: F = a_0 ∏ (X − α_i Y) with distinct α_i. Put ξ = x/y and choose i with |ξ − α_i| minimal; then |ξ − α_j| ≥ |α_i − α_j|/2 for j ≠ i.
roth-lower-bound-for-all-algebraic-numbers: |ξ − α_i| ≥ c(α_i, κ) H(ξ)^{-κ} ≥ c(α_i, κ) max(|x|, |y|)^{-κ} (H(ξ) ≤ max(|x|, |y|); ξ ≠ α_i as F(x, y) ≠ 0).
|F(x, y)| = |y|^d |a_0| ∏_j |ξ − α_j| ≥ c(α_i, κ) |a_0| ∏_{j ≠ i} (|α_i − α_j|/2) max(|x|, |y|)^{d−κ}; take c(F, κ) the minimum over i.
acceptance: For d ≤ 2 the statement holds trivially since |F(x, y)| ≥ 1 (Evertse's remark); the node keeps d ≥ 3 as the source.
The constant c(F, κ) is not effectively computable (it comes from Roth's theorem).

nodes.title: A square-free divisor of degree ≥ 3 (the reduction in Evertse, Corollary 6.4)
nodes.statement: Let F ∈ ℤ[X, Y] be a binary form such that F(X, 1) has at least three distinct complex roots. Then F is divisible in ℤ[X, Y] by a square-free binary form F* ∈ ℤ[X, Y] of degree ≥ 3.
hypotheses: F homogeneous with integer coefficients
F(X, 1) has ≥ 3 distinct roots in ℂ
proofSteps: Factor F(X, 1) = c g_1^{k_1} ··· g_t^{k_t} with g_i ∈ ℤ[X] irreducible, primitive and pairwise non-associate; put f* = g_1 ··· g_t, of degree d* ≥ 3 (it has the same roots as F(X, 1)) with distinct roots.
F(X, 1) = f* g with g ∈ ℤ[X] (Gauss's lemma, Polynomial.IsPrimitive.Int.dvd_iff_map_cast_dvd_map_cast); set F*(X, Y) = Y^{d*} f*(X/Y) and G(X, Y) = Y^{deg F − d*} g(X/Y), so F = F* G.
F* is square-free: f* has d* distinct roots and F*(1, 0) = leading coefficient of f* ≠ 0, so F* = a ∏ (X − α_i Y) with distinct α_i.
acceptance: The source writes F*(X, Y) = Y^d f(X/Y) for Y^d f*(X/Y) (misprint recorded).

nodes.title: Thue's theorem: Thue equations have finitely many solutions (Evertse, Corollary 6.4)
nodes.statement: Let F ∈ ℤ[X, Y] be a binary form such that F(X, 1) has at least three distinct roots in ℂ, and let m be a nonzero integer. Then F(x, y) = m has only finitely many solutions (x, y) ∈ ℤ^2. The proof is ineffective; effective bounds for the solutions are stage DT.4's theorem DT.4/thue-equation-effective-bound.
hypotheses: F homogeneous with integer coefficients
F(X, 1) has ≥ 3 distinct roots
proofSteps: squarefree-divisor-of-binary-form: F = F* G with F* square-free of degree d ≥ 3; for a solution, F*(x, y) divides m, so 0 < |F*(x, y)| ≤ |m|.
Take 2 < κ < d; binary-form-lower-bound gives |m| ≥ c(F*, κ) max(|x|, |y|)^{d−κ}, so max(|x|, |y|) is bounded and the solutions are finite.
acceptance: x^3 − 2y^3 = 1 has finitely many integer solutions.
Degree 2 fails: Pell equations x^2 − 2y^2 = 1 have infinitely many solutions (F(X, 1) has only two roots).
Pottmeyer, Theorem 3.1.3 proves the analogue over rings of integers of number fields (degree > 2[K : ℚ]) from the number-field form of Roth; that form is not part of this stage.

nodes.title: Linear forms in general position
nodes.statement: Let F be a field, n ≥ 1 an integer and ι a finite index type. A linear form in X_1, …, X_n with coefficients in F is identified with its coefficient vector: L = α_1X_1 + ⋯ + α_nX_n ↔ α = (α_1, …, α_n) ∈ F^n, and L(x) := α · x = Σ_j α_j x_j (the dot product) for x ∈ F^n (and, by coercion, for x ∈ ℤ^n when ℤ → F). A family L = (L_i)_{i ∈ ι} of such forms is in general position if every n-element subfamily is linearly independent over F: for every S ⊆ ι with #S = n, the vectors (L_i)_{i ∈ S} are linearly independent in F^n, equivalently det(α_{ij})_{i ∈ S, 1 ≤ j ≤ n} ≠ 0 for any ordering of S. Convention pinned: when #ι < n the condition is vacuous, but every use below has #ι ≥ n (Evertse writes r ≥ n); when #ι = n it is linear independence of L.
hypotheses: F a field; n ≥ 1; ι a finite type (the source's r = #ι ≥ n)
Linear forms are coefficient vectors in F^n evaluated by the dot product; this matches Mathlib's `dotProduct` (notation ⬝ᵥ)
Linear (in)dependence is over F; for forms with algebraic coefficients in ℂ, independence over ℂ and over Q̄ coincide (both mean the determinant is non-zero)
proofSteps: Define InGeneralPosition L :⇔ ∀ S : Finset ι, #S = n → LinearIndependent F (fun i : S ↦ L i).
The determinant characterisation follows from Mathlib's Matrix.linearIndependent_rows_iff_isUnit applied to the n × n matrix whose rows are the L_i, i ∈ S.
acceptance: For n = 2 and ι = {1, 2, 3} the forms X_1, X_2, X_1 + X_2 over ℚ are in general position.
The forms X_1, X_2, X_1 + X_2, X_3 (n = 3) are pairwise independent but not in general position, since X_1, X_2, X_1 + X_2 are dependent.

nodes.title: Coordinates are bounded by n independent linear forms (Evertse Lemmas 7.5 and 8.9)
nodes.statement: Let F be a field with an absolute value |·|_* (Mathlib `AbsoluteValue F ℝ`), n ≥ 1, and M_1, …, M_n linearly independent linear forms in X_1, …, X_n with coefficients in F. Then there is C' > 0 such that for all x = (x_1, …, x_n) ∈ F^n, max_{1≤k≤n} |x_k|_* ≤ C' · max_{1≤j≤n} |M_j(x)|_*. One may take C' := max(1, max_k Σ_j |β_{kj}|_*), where (β_{kj}) is the inverse of the coefficient matrix of M_1, …, M_n, so that X_k = Σ_j β_{kj} M_j.
hypotheses: |·|_* is any absolute value on F (archimedean or not), e.g. |·| on ℂ (Lemma 7.5) or a continuation of |·|_p to a number field (Lemma 8.9)
M_1, …, M_n linearly independent over F (coefficient determinant non-zero)
proofSteps: The coefficient matrix A = (α_{jk}) of M_1, …, M_n is invertible (Matrix.linearIndependent_rows_iff_isUnit); put B := A⁻¹ = (β_{kj}). Then x = B(Ax) (Matrix.nonsing_inv_mul), i.e. x_k = Σ_j β_{kj} M_j(x).
By the triangle inequality and multiplicativity of |·|_*, |x_k|_* ≤ Σ_j |β_{kj}|_* |M_j(x)|_* ≤ (Σ_j |β_{kj}|_*) · max_j |M_j(x)|_*.
Take the maximum over k; replacing the constant by its maximum with 1 makes it positive.
acceptance: For M_j = X_j (A the identity) the lemma holds with C' = 1.
For F = ℚ, |·|_* = |·|_p and M_1 = X_1 + X_2, M_2 = X_2: x_1 = M_1 − M_2 and max(|x_1|_p, |x_2|_p) ≤ 2 max(|M_1(x)|_p, |M_2(x)|_p) (in fact ≤ 1 · max by the ultrametric inequality).

nodes.title: Hadamard's inequality
nodes.statement: For vectors a_1, …, a_n ∈ ℂ^n (n ≥ 1), |det(a_1, …, a_n)| ≤ ∏_{j=1}^n ‖a_j‖_2, where ‖a‖_2 = (Σ_i |a_i|^2)^{1/2} is the Euclidean norm. In particular, for linear forms L_1, …, L_n with complex coefficients, |det(L_1, …, L_n)| ≤ ∏ ‖L_j‖_2 (coefficient vectors), and |det(x_1, …, x_p) minors| ≤ ∏‖x_j‖_2 for the Plücker coordinates of p vectors.
hypotheses: Vectors in ℂ^n with the standard Hermitian inner product; determinant of the matrix with columns a_j
proofSteps: If a_1, …, a_n are linearly dependent both sides compare trivially (det = 0).

Otherwise apply Gram–Schmidt (InnerProductSpace.gramSchmidt): b_j = a_j − Σ_{i<j} proj_{b_i}(a_j) are pairwise orthogonal (InnerProductSpace.gramSchmidt_orthogonal), and the matrix (b_1, …, b_n) = (a_1, …, a_n)·U with U unipotent upper triangular, so det(b) = det(a) (Matrix.det_mul, determinant of a unitriangular matrix is 1).
Since the b_j are orthogonal, B*B = diag(‖b_j‖²), so |det B|² = det(B*B) = ∏‖b_j‖².
By Pythagoras ‖b_j‖ ≤ ‖a_j‖ (b_j is a_j minus its orthogonal projection onto span(b_1, …, b_{j−1})). Combine.
acceptance: Equality for orthogonal columns: det(e_1, …, e_n) = 1 = ∏‖e_j‖.

sources.match: The use of Hadamard's inequality at infinite places (the n^{n s(w)/2} factor comes from comparing ‖·‖_2 with the maximum norm).

nodes.title: Continuations of the absolute values of ℚ to a number field exist
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field. (a) For every prime p there is an absolute value |·|_𝔭 on K with |q|_𝔭 = |q|_p for all q ∈ ℚ (a continuation of the p-adic absolute value, normalised by |p|_p = p⁻¹). (b) There is an absolute value |·|_∞ on K with |q|_∞ = |q| for all q ∈ ℚ. Concretely, (a) x ↦ ‖τ(x)‖ for any field embedding τ : K → PadicAlgCl p (a fixed algebraic closure of ℚ_p with its spectral norm), and (b) x ↦ |σ(x)| for any field embedding σ : K → ℂ.
hypotheses: K a number field; p prime
Normalisation |p|_p = p⁻¹ (Mathlib padicNorm, Rat.AbsoluteValue.padic)
proofSteps: K/ℚ is algebraic and PadicAlgCl p is algebraically closed of characteristic 0, so there is a ℚ-algebra embedding τ : K → PadicAlgCl p (IsAlgClosed.lift); similarly σ : K → ℂ.
x ↦ ‖τ(x)‖ is an absolute value on K (the norm on the field PadicAlgCl p is multiplicative and satisfies the triangle inequality).
For q ∈ ℚ: ‖τ(q)‖ = ‖(q : ℚ_p)‖ (PadicAlgCl.norm_extends) = padicNorm p q (padicNormE.eq_padic_norm'). For (b), |σ(q)| = |q|.
Evertse constructs the same continuations from prime ideal factorisation, |x|_𝔭 := p^{−k/e(𝔭)} (Lemma 8.5); either construction serves every use in this stage, which needs only existence.
acceptance: For K = ℚ the continuation in (a) is |·|_p itself.
For K = ℚ(i) and p = 5, the two embeddings i ↦ ±√−1 ∈ ℚ_5 (which exists since −1 is a square mod 5) give the two continuations |·|_{𝔭}, |·|_{𝔭̄} with |2 + i| = 5⁻¹ at exactly one of them.

nodes.title: Every continuation of |·|_p to a number field extends to Q̄
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field, Q̄ an algebraic closure of K, and |·|_v an absolute value on K whose restriction to ℚ is |·|_p for a prime p, or is |·| (p = ∞). Then there is a field embedding τ : Q̄ → PadicAlgCl p (resp. τ : Q̄ → ℂ) with |x|_v = ‖τ(x)‖ (resp. |τ(x)|) for all x ∈ K; in particular |·|_v extends to the absolute value x ↦ ‖τ(x)‖ on Q̄. Equivalently: every continuation of |·|_p to K is of the form x ↦ ‖τ(x)‖ for a ℚ-embedding τ : K → PadicAlgCl p.
hypotheses: K a number field; |·|_v an absolute value on K with |q|_v = |q|_p (q ∈ ℚ), p a prime or p = ∞
proofSteps: Case p prime: complete K at |·|_v to K_v; the closure of ℚ in K_v is ℚ_p and K_v = ℚ_p · K is a finite extension of ℚ_p. Choose a ℚ_p-embedding ι : K_v → PadicAlgCl p (IsAlgClosed.lift).

Both |·|_v (extended by continuity to K_v) and x ↦ ‖ι(x)‖ are absolute values on the algebraic extension K_v/ℚ_p extending ‖·‖ on the complete field ℚ_p, so they coincide with the spectral norm (spectralNorm_unique_field_norm_ext); hence |x|_v = ‖ι(x)‖ on K.
Extend ι|_K : K → PadicAlgCl p to τ : Q̄ → PadicAlgCl p (IsAlgClosed.lift, Q̄/K algebraic).

Case p=∞ requires a norm-preserving classification of completions of number fields as ℝ or ℂ. The previously cited complex Gelfand–Mazur map assumes an existing NormedAlgebra ℂ structure and does not by itself construct this classification (or the real case). Once that classification is supplied, obtain σ:K→ℂ preserving |·|_v and extend it to Q̄ by IsAlgClosed.lift. This infrastructure is a recorded gap.

This is the source's 'Fact' that the |·|_{σ_i} and |·|_{𝔭_i} are precisely the continuations; the source states it without proof, and the proof above is the standard one (Neukirch, Algebraic Number Theory, Ch. II, §4 and §8).
acceptance: For K = ℚ(√2) and p = 7 (2 is a square mod 7), the two continuations of |·|_7 correspond to the two embeddings √2 ↦ ±√2 ∈ ℚ_7.
For K ⊂ ℂ and |·|_v the restriction of |·|, the embedding τ can be taken to extend the inclusion K ⊂ ℂ.

nodes.title: S-units of ℚ via the product of absolute values (Evertse Lemma 8.11)
nodes.statement: Let p_1, …, p_s be distinct primes and u ∈ ℚ. Then u = ±p_1^{w_1} ⋯ p_s^{w_s} for some w_1, …, w_s ∈ ℤ if and only if |u| · |u|_{p_1} ⋯ |u|_{p_s} = 1. More generally, for every non-zero integer g, |g| · ∏_{j} |g|_{p_j} = ∏_{q ∉ {p_1,…,p_s}} q^{v_q(g)} ≥ 1.
hypotheses: p_1, …, p_s distinct primes (s ≥ 0)
u ∈ ℚ; |·|_p normalised by |p|_p = p⁻¹
proofSteps: If u = 0 both sides fail (the product is 0).

If u ≠ 0 write u = ±∏_q q^{v_q(u)} over all primes (factorisation of numerator and denominator). Then |u| = ∏_q q^{v_q(u)} and |u|_{p_j} = p_j^{−v_{p_j}(u)} (padicNorm.eq_zpow_of_nonzero), so |u| ∏_j |u|_{p_j} = ∏_{q ∉ S} q^{v_q(u)}.
By uniqueness of prime factorisation this product equals 1 iff v_q(u) = 0 for all q ∉ S, i.e. iff u = ±∏_j p_j^{v_{p_j}(u)}.
For a non-zero integer g all v_q(g) ≥ 0, whence the inequality ≥ 1.

nodes.title: Schmidt's Subspace Theorem (Evertse Theorem 7.1)
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 2, let L_i = α_{i1}X_1 + ⋯ + α_{in}X_n (i = 1, …, n) be n linearly independent linear forms with coefficients α_{ij} ∈ Q̄ ⊂ ℂ (algebraic complex numbers), and let C > 0, δ > 0. For x ∈ ℤ^n put ‖x‖ := max(|x_1|, …, |x_n|). Then there are finitely many proper linear subspaces T_1, …, T_t of ℚ^n such that every solution x ∈ ℤ^n of |L_1(x) ⋯ L_n(x)| ≤ C‖x‖^{−δ} (7.1) lies in T_1 ∪ ⋯ ∪ T_t (ℤ^n ⊂ ℚ^n). The subspaces T_i are the exceptional subspaces; the theorem asserts their existence only: the known proofs are ineffective and do not determine them, while the number t can be bounded explicitly (quantitative Subspace Theorem).
hypotheses: α_{ij} ∈ ℂ algebraic over ℚ
det(α_{ij}) ≠ 0 (linear independence over ℂ, equivalently over Q̄)
‖x‖ is the maximum norm; x = 0 is a solution and lies in every subspace
The conclusion is containment in finitely many proper subspaces, not finiteness of the solution set (see vanishing-form-gives-infinitely-many-solutions and exceptional-subspace-example-three-forms)
proofSteps: Let K := ℚ(α_{ij} : 1 ≤ i, j ≤ n) ⊂ ℂ, a number field, and let |·|_∞ be the restriction to K of the absolute value of ℂ; it is a continuation of the standard absolute value of ℚ.

Apply the p-adic Subspace Theorem (Evertse Theorem 8.7) with this K, with s = 0 (no primes), and with L_{i,∞} := L_i. Inequality (8.7) is then literally (7.1), and its conclusion is the conclusion here.
acceptance: DT.2 acceptance: the exceptional finite union T_1 ∪ ⋯ ∪ T_t is part of the conclusion, and finiteness of t is separate from effectivity: nothing in the statement or proof determines the T_i.
Case n = 2 with L_1 = Y, L_2 = X − αY gives Roth's theorem (roth-from-subspace-theorem).
Degenerate check: if L_1(x_0) = 0 for some non-zero x_0 ∈ ℤ^n, then all λx_0 are solutions, so the solution set can be infinite; they lie in the one subspace ℚx_0.
Non-example of the finiteness strengthening: for (7.5) with 0 < δ < 1 there are infinitely many solutions even with 0 < |L_1L_2L_3|, all in x_3 = 0.

nodes.title: Subspace Theorem for r ≥ n forms in general position (Evertse Theorem 7.4)
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 2, r ≥ n, and let L_i = α_{i1}X_1 + ⋯ + α_{in}X_n (i = 1, …, r) be linear forms with coefficients in Q̄ ⊂ ℂ in general position, and C > 0, δ > 0. Then the set of solutions x ∈ ℤ^n of |L_1(x) ⋯ L_r(x)| ≤ C‖x‖^{r−n−δ} (7.6) is contained in a union of finitely many proper linear subspaces of ℚ^n. The case r = n is Theorem 7.1, so the two theorems are equivalent.
hypotheses: n ≥ 2, r ≥ n
α_{ij} ∈ ℂ algebraic
L_1, …, L_r in general position
proofSteps: Partition the solutions x ≠ 0 into r! classes according to a permutation π with |L_{π(1)}(x)| ≤ ⋯ ≤ |L_{π(r)}(x)|; it suffices to treat each class, say π = id: |L_1(x)| ≤ ⋯ ≤ |L_r(x)| (7.7).

For i ∈ {n+1, …, r} the forms L_1, …, L_{n−1}, L_i are linearly independent (general position), so by sup-norm-bounded-by-independent-forms there is C_i with ‖x‖ ≤ C_i max(|L_1(x)|, …, |L_{n−1}(x)|, |L_i(x)|) = C_i|L_i(x)| on the class.
For x ≠ 0 in the class, L_i(x) ≠ 0 for i > n: otherwise |L_1(x)| = ⋯ = |L_n(x)| = 0 and x = 0 since L_1, …, L_n are independent.

L_1, …, L_n are linearly independent (general position), so Theorem 7.1 (subspace-theorem-and-its-exceptional-subspaces) puts the class into finitely many proper subspaces; x = 0 lies in any of them. Take the union over the r! classes.
Converse: for r = n, general position is linear independence and (7.6) is (7.1).
acceptance: r = n recovers Theorem 7.1.

The norm form application: for α_1, …, α_n ∈ K with the d conjugate forms in general position and d > n, the solutions of |N_{K/ℚ}(α·x)| ≤ C‖x‖^{d−n−δ} lie in finitely many proper subspaces (used in Theorem 7.9).

nodes.title: Schlickewei's p-adic Subspace Theorem (Evertse Theorem 8.7)
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field, p_1, …, p_s distinct primes (s ≥ 0), and for each p ∈ {∞, p_1, …, p_s} fix a continuation |·|_p to K of the absolute value |·|_p of ℚ (|·|_∞ the ordinary one, |p|_p = p⁻¹). Let n ≥ 2, ε > 0, C > 0, and for each p ∈ {∞, p_1, …, p_s} let L_{1,p}, …, L_{n,p} be linearly independent linear forms in X_1, …, X_n with coefficients in K. Then there are finitely many proper linear subspaces T_1, …, T_t of ℚ^n such that every solution x ∈ ℤ^n of |L_{1,∞}(x) ⋯ L_{n,∞}(x)|_∞ · ∏_{j=1}^s |L_{1,p_j}(x) ⋯ L_{n,p_j}(x)|_{p_j} ≤ C‖x‖^{−ε} (8.7) lies in T_1 ∪ ⋯ ∪ T_t. The only known proofs are ineffective.
hypotheses: K a number field; p_1, …, p_s distinct primes, s ≥ 0
|·|_p (p ∈ {∞, p_1, …, p_s}) continuations to K of the absolute values of ℚ (notation (8.4))
n ≥ 2; for each p the n forms L_{i,p} ∈ K[X_1, …, X_n] are linearly independent
‖x‖ = max_i |x_i| (maximum norm)
proofSteps: Reduction to primitive points: if x = g x' with g = gcd(x) ≥ 1 and x' primitive, then the left side of (8.7) at x equals |g|^n ∏_j |g|_{p_j}^n times its value at x', and |g| ∏_j |g|_{p_j} ≥ 1 (rational-s-unit-product-criterion), while ‖x'‖ ≤ ‖x‖; so x' is a solution, and x, x' lie in the same subspaces. x = 0 lies in every subspace. Replace ε by min(ε,1) before the reduction to systems: for ‖x‖≥1 the original solutions are a subset of those with that weaker positive exponent.

Extend each |·|_p from K to Q̄ (absolute-value-extends-to-algebraic-closure). Work over the base field ℚ with S := {∞, p_1, …, p_s}; the normalised absolute values of ℚ are ‖·‖_p = |·|_p, the forms L_{i,p} have coefficients in K ⊂ Q̄, and for primitive x ∈ ℤ^n one has ‖x‖_p = 1 for all primes p and H(x) = ‖x‖ (Rat.mulHeight_eq_max_abs_of_gcd_eq_one).
Solutions with L_{i,p}(x) = 0 for some (i, p): {y ∈ ℚ^n : L_{i,p}(y) = 0} is a proper subspace of ℚ^n (L_{i,p} ≠ 0 and ℚ^n spans K^n), giving at most n(s+1) subspaces.

For the remaining primitive solutions with ‖x‖ ≥ B, product-inequality-reduces-to-systems gives finitely many exponent tuples (d_{ip}) with d_{ip} ≤ 0, Σ_{p,i} d_{ip} = −n − ε/2, such that each solution satisfies one system |L_{i,p}(x)|_p/‖x‖_p ≤ A_{ip} H(x)^{d_{ip}} (all i, p).

Each such system is EF's system (3.7) over the base field ℚ (for x ∈ ℚ^n all Galois conjugates σ(x) equal x), with ε/2 in place of ε; by absolute-subspace-theorem-for-systems its solutions x with H(x) ≥ C_1 lie in finitely many proper subspaces of Q̄^n defined over ℚ, whose ℚ-points are proper subspaces of ℚ^n.
The primitive solutions with ‖x‖ < max(B, C_1) are finitely many integer points, each in a proper line ℚx (n ≥ 2). Collect all subspaces.
acceptance: s = 0 is Theorem 7.1.
DT.2 acceptance: exceptional finite union at theorem level; ineffective.

Example (Evertse (8.8)): with K = ℚ and the primes 2, 3, 5, the solutions of |2^u + 3^v − 5^w| ≤ max(2^u, 3^v, 5^w)^{1−ε} give points x = (2^u, 3^v, 5^w) lying in finitely many proper subspaces of ℚ³ (apply the theorem to (x_1 + x_2 − x_3)x_1x_2 at ∞ and x_1x_2x_3 at 2, 3, 5 on the part with ‖x‖ = |x_3|).

sources.match: The statement (continued with (8.7) and the conclusion 'There are a finite number of proper linear subspaces T1, . . . , Tt of Qn such that all solutions of (8.7) lie in T1 ∪ · · · ∪ Tt').

The route of the proof: reduction to systems, then Theorem 3.1.

nodes.title: p-adic Subspace Theorem for forms in general position (Evertse Theorem 8.8)
nodes.statement: Keep notation (8.4) and let n ≥ 2, ε > 0, C > 0. For each p ∈ {∞, p_1, …, p_s} let L_{1,p}, …, L_{r_p,p} (r_p ≥ n) be linear forms in X_1, …, X_n with coefficients in K in general position. Then there are finitely many proper linear subspaces T_1, …, T_t of ℚ^n containing all solutions x ∈ ℤ^n with gcd(x_1, …, x_n) = 1 of |L_{1,∞}(x) ⋯ L_{r_∞,∞}(x)|_∞ · ∏_{j=1}^s |L_{1,p_j}(x) ⋯ L_{r_{p_j},p_j}(x)|_{p_j} ≤ C‖x‖^{r_∞ − n − ε} (8.9).
hypotheses: Notation (8.4)
n ≥ 2; r_p ≥ n forms at each p, in general position
Solutions are primitive integer vectors
The exponent on the right involves r_∞ only
proofSteps: For each solution and each p choose a permutation σ_p ordering |L_{σ_p(1),p}(x)|_p ≤ ⋯ ≤ |L_{σ_p(r_p),p}(x)|_p; finitely many choices of (σ_p)_p, so it suffices to treat one, say σ_p = id for all p.
For i > n the forms L_{1,p}, …, L_{n−1,p}, L_{i,p} are independent, so sup-norm-bounded-by-independent-forms (Lemma 8.9) gives C_{i,p} with max_k |x_k|_p ≤ C_{i,p}|L_{i,p}(x)|_p.

For p = ∞, max_k |x_k|_∞ = ‖x‖; for p = p_j, since gcd(x) = 1 some x_k is a p-adic unit and max_k |x_k|_p = 1. Hence ‖x‖ ≤ C_{i,∞}|L_{i,∞}(x)| and 1 ≤ C_{i,p_j}|L_{i,p_j}(x)|_{p_j} for i > n (in particular these values are non-zero).
Inserting into (8.9): ∏_p |L_{1,p}(x) ⋯ L_{n,p}(x)|_p ≤ C'' ‖x‖^{−ε} with C'' = C ∏_{p, i>n} C_{i,p}; apply p-adic-subspace-theorem to the independent forms L_{1,p}, …, L_{n,p}.
acceptance: r_p = n at every p gives Theorem 8.7 for primitive solutions.
The forms Y_1, …, Y_n, Y_1 + ⋯ + Y_n (r_p = n + 1) are in general position; this is the instance used in Lemma 8.15.

nodes.title: Reduction of the product inequality to finitely many systems (Mahler; Evertse–Schlickewei §21)
nodes.statement: Keep notation (8.4), let n ≥ 2, 0 < ε ≤ 1, C > 0, and for each p ∈ S := {∞, p_1, …, p_s} let L_{1,p}, …, L_{n,p} be linearly independent forms with coefficients in K. Put A_{ip} := n · max(1, max_j |α^{(p)}_{ij}|_p) where L_{i,p} = Σ_j α^{(p)}_{ij}X_j, so that |L_{i,p}(x)|_p ≤ A_{ip}‖x‖_p for x ∈ ℤ^n (‖x‖_∞ = ‖x‖, ‖x‖_p = max_j|x_j|_p). Then there are a real B ≥ 1 and a finite set D of tuples d = (d_{ip})_{p ∈ S, 1 ≤ i ≤ n} of reals with d_{ip} ≤ 0 and Σ_{p,i} d_{ip} = −n − ε/2, such that every primitive x ∈ ℤ^n with ‖x‖ ≥ B, with L_{i,p}(x) ≠ 0 for all (i, p), and satisfying (8.7), satisfies for some d ∈ D the system |L_{i,p}(x)|_p ≤ A_{ip}‖x‖_p ‖x‖^{d_{ip}} for all p ∈ S and i = 1, …, n.
hypotheses: Notation (8.4); n ≥ 2; 0 < ε ≤ 1; C > 0
Forms at each place linearly independent
Solutions primitive, with all L_{i,p}(x) ≠ 0 (the others lie in the proper subspaces L_{i,p} = 0)
proofSteps: Apply finite-simplex-discretisation with q=n(s+1) and the γ chosen below. The lemma separately records the finite grid and its domination property; no sharper cardinality bound is required.
Choose B≥2, large enough for the logarithmic estimate below. For a solution x put y_{ip} ≥ 0 by |L_{i,p}(x)|_p/(A_{ip}‖x‖_p) = ‖x‖^{−y_{ip}} (possible since the left side is in (0, 1]).
For primitive x, ∏_{p ∈ S} ‖x‖_p^n = ‖x‖^n, so (8.7) gives ‖x‖^{−Σ y_{ip}} ≤ C (∏ A_{ip})^{−1} ‖x‖^{−n−ε}, i.e. Σ y_{ip} ≥ n + ε − log(C/∏A_{ip})/log‖x‖ ≥ n + 3ε/4 once ‖x‖ ≥ B.

Apply the grid lemma with q = n(s+1) and γ := (n + ε/2)/(n + 3ε/4) ∈ [1/2, 1): y_{ip} ≥ Γ_{ip}Σy ≥ Γ_{ip}(n + 3ε/4). Put d_{ip} := −Γ_{ip}(n + 3ε/4) ≤ 0; then Σ d_{ip} = −γ(n + 3ε/4) = −n − ε/2 and ‖x‖^{−y_{ip}} ≤ ‖x‖^{d_{ip}}. The set D of such d is finite since J' is.
acceptance: s=0,n=2, forms Y and X−αY: the systems are |y|≤2‖x‖^(1+d₁), |x−αy|≤A‖x‖^(1+d₂), with d₁+d₂=−2−ε/2. The norm factor in the theorem must be retained.
The number of systems depends only on n, s, ε (through q and γ), not on the forms.

nodes.title: Vojta's refinement: effectively computable exceptional subspaces (Evertse Theorem 7.14)
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 2, r ≥ n and L_1, …, L_r linear forms in X_1, …, X_n with coefficients in Q̄ ⊂ ℂ in general position. Then there is a finite, effectively computable collection U_1, …, U_s of proper linear subspaces of ℚ^n, depending only on L_1, …, L_r, such that for every C > 0 and δ > 0 the inequality |L_1(x) ⋯ L_r(x)| ≤ C‖x‖^{r−n−δ} has only finitely many solutions x ∈ ℤ^n outside U_1 ∪ ⋯ ∪ U_s. The subspaces are fixed as C, δ vary; the finite set of solutions outside them depends on C, δ and cannot be determined effectively by the known proofs.
hypotheses: n ≥ 2, r ≥ n; forms with algebraic complex coefficients in general position
'Effectively computable' refers to the subspaces only, not to the finitely many remaining solutions
proofSteps: For the proof replace δ by min(δ,1), since every integer x≠0 has ‖x‖≥1 and the original inequality implies this weaker positive-exponent inequality. The product-to-systems lemma and interval refinement can then be used within their 0<ε≤1 ranges. The final exceptional collection depends only on the forms, not this reduction.

As in the proof of subspace-theorem-general-position, for each of the r! orderings the solutions with that ordering satisfy |L_{π(1)}(x) ⋯ L_{π(n)}(x)| ≤ C'‖x‖^{−δ} with L_{π(1)}, …, L_{π(n)} independent.

By product-inequality-reduces-to-systems (s = 0, K := ℚ(coefficients) ⊂ ℂ), primitive solutions of each such inequality with large ‖x‖ and non-vanishing forms satisfy one of finitely many systems (3.7) over the base field ℚ with S = {∞} and exponents d_i ≤ 0, Σ d_i = −n − δ/2; solutions where a form vanishes lie in the subspaces L_i = 0, which are among the kernels of the forms.

By faltings-wustholz-interval-refinement (EF Theorem 3.3), each system has an exceptional proper subspace T, effectively computable and belonging to a finite collection depending only on the forms L_{π(1)}, …, L_{π(n)}, such that solutions outside T have bounded height; hence finitely many integer solutions outside T.

Let U_1, …, U_s be the ℚ-rational parts of all subspaces in these finite collections (over all n-subsets of {L_1, …, L_r}) together with the kernels L_i = 0; this depends only on L_1, …, L_r. Outside their union, each primitive solution lies outside the T of its system, so only finitely many primitive solutions remain. A solution x = g·x' (g = gcd(x) ≥ 1) makes x' a solution, and since the L_i(x') are non-zero outside the kernels, g^{n+δ} ≤ C‖x'‖^{r−n−δ}/|L_1(x') ⋯ L_r(x')| bounds g; so finitely many solutions remain in total.
acceptance: Exercise 7.1 of the source: for (7.5) the collection may be taken to be the three planes x_1 = 0, x_2 = 0, x_3 = 0.
Finiteness separated from effectivity: U_1, …, U_s are effective, the solutions outside them are not.

nodes.title: A form vanishing at an integer point gives infinitely many solutions in one line
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 2, L_1, …, L_n linear forms with complex coefficients, C > 0, δ > 0. If L_i(x_0) = 0 for some i and some non-zero x_0 ∈ ℤ^n, then every λx_0 (λ ∈ ℤ) is a solution of |L_1(x) ⋯ L_n(x)| ≤ C‖x‖^{−δ} (7.1); these infinitely many solutions lie in the proper subspace ℚx_0. Hence the conclusion of the Subspace Theorem cannot be strengthened to finiteness of the solution set of (7.1).
hypotheses: n ≥ 2; x_0 ∈ ℤ^n non-zero with L_i(x_0) = 0 for some i
proofSteps: L_i(λx_0) = λL_i(x_0) = 0, so the left side of (7.1) vanishes at λx_0 for every λ ∈ ℤ.
The points λx_0 are pairwise distinct and lie in ℚx_0, a proper subspace since n ≥ 2.
acceptance: L_1 = X_1, L_2 = X_2 (n = 2) and x_0 = (0, 1): every (0, λ), λ ∈ ℤ, is a solution of (7.1), all in the line x_1 = 0.
This is why the strict version 0 < |L_1(x) ⋯ L_n(x)| (7.3) is introduced.

nodes.title: Infinitely many solutions of the strict inequality inside one subspace (Evertse Example (7.5))
nodes.statement: Let 0 < δ < 1. The inequality 0 < |(x_1 + √2x_2 + √3x_3)(x_1 − √2x_2 + √3x_3)(x_1 − √2x_2 − √3x_3)| ≤ ‖x‖^{−δ} (7.5) in x ∈ ℤ³ has infinitely many solutions with x_3 = 0, although its three linear forms are linearly independent (determinant 4√6). Hence for n ≥ 3 even the strict version 0 < |L_1(x) ⋯ L_n(x)| ≤ C‖x‖^{−δ} (7.3) may have infinitely many solutions, and the exceptional subspaces in the Subspace Theorem are necessary.
hypotheses: Solutions x = (x_1, x_2, 0) with x_1x_2 ≠ 0
proofSteps: By Dirichlet (Real.infinite_rat_abs_sub_lt_one_div_den_sq_of_irrational with irrational_sqrt_two) there are infinitely many rationals x_1/x_2 in lowest terms, x_2 > 0, with |√2 − x_1/x_2| < x_2^{−2}; for all but finitely many of them x_1 ≠ 0.
The product is non-zero because √2 is irrational and x_2 ≠ 0; distinct fractions give distinct points. Only finitely many fractions have ‖x‖ below the bound.
The determinant of the three coefficient vectors (1, √2, √3), (1, −√2, √3), (1, −√2, −√3) is 4√6 ≠ 0.
acceptance: Degenerate comparison: for n = 2 the strict inequality has only finitely many solutions (two-form-strict-inequality-finite), so n ≥ 3 is essential.
Exercise 7.1 of the source: the solutions also fill the planes x_1 = 0 and x_2 = 0, and only finitely many solutions have x_1x_2x_3 ≠ 0 (a check of Vojta's refinement).

nodes.title: For two forms the strict inequality has finitely many solutions (Evertse Lemma 7.3)
nodes.statement: Let L_i = α_{i1}X + α_{i2}Y (i = 1, 2) be two linearly independent linear forms with coefficients in Q̄ ⊂ ℂ and C > 0, δ > 0. Then 0 < |L_1(x)L_2(x)| ≤ C‖x‖^{−δ} (7.4) has only finitely many solutions x = (x, y) ∈ ℤ².
hypotheses: Two independent forms in two variables with algebraic coefficients
proofSteps: By subspace-theorem-and-its-exceptional-subspaces the solutions lie in finitely many one-dimensional subspaces T = ℚx_0 of ℚ², x_0 = (x_0, y_0) ∈ ℤ² primitive, so the integer points of T are λx_0 with λ ∈ ℤ.
If L_1(x_0)L_2(x_0) = 0 then T contains no solution of the strict inequality.
Otherwise λx_0 is a solution iff 0 < λ²|L_1(x_0)L_2(x_0)| ≤ C|λ|^{−δ}‖x_0‖^{−δ}, i.e. |λ|^{2+δ} ≤ C‖x_0‖^{−δ}|L_1(x_0)L_2(x_0)|^{−1}, which bounds |λ|.
acceptance: Contrast with exceptional-subspace-example-three-forms: for three forms in three variables the strict inequality can have infinitely many solutions.

For L₁=X, L₂=Y and C=1, every δ>0 gives exactly the four solutions (±1,±1). Their norm and nonzero product both equal 1. For norm greater than 1 the right-hand side is below 1, so there are no other solutions.

nodes.title: Roth's theorem deduced from the Subspace Theorem (Evertse Corollary 7.2)
nodes.statement: Let α ∈ Q̄ ⊂ ℂ be algebraic, C > 0 and κ > 2. Then |ξ − α| ≤ C·H(ξ)^{−κ} (7.2) has only finitely many solutions ξ ∈ ℚ, where H(x/y) := max(|x|, |y|) for coprime x, y ∈ ℤ (Mathlib's Height.mulHeight₁ on ℚ, by Rat.mulHeight₁_eq_max). Like the Subspace Theorem, the proof is ineffective: it bounds neither the size of the solutions nor gives a way to list them.
hypotheses: α algebraic over ℚ (real or not; rational α allowed)
H is the naive height of a rational number, H(x/y) = max(|x|, |y|) in lowest terms
proofSteps: Let ξ = x/y (gcd(x, y) = 1, y ≠ 0) be a solution and write κ = 2 + δ, δ > 0. Multiplying (7.2) by y² gives |y(x − αy)| ≤ Cy² max(|x|, |y|)^{−2−δ} ≤ C max(|x|, |y|)^{−δ} = C‖(x, y)‖^{−δ}.

The forms Y and X − αY are linearly independent with algebraic coefficients, so by subspace-theorem-and-its-exceptional-subspaces the pairs (x, y) lie in finitely many one-dimensional subspaces of ℚ².
A one-dimensional subspace ℚ(x_0, y_0) determines the fraction x/y uniquely (and the subspace y = 0 contains no solution since y ≠ 0). Hence finitely many ξ.
acceptance: Compatibility with DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.1/roth-theorem: for real algebraic α of degree ≥ 3 and C = 1 this is Roth's theorem in the form of Evertse Theorem 6.2.
Theorem 7.7 with n = 2 gives a second deduction for irrational α (see single-linear-form-inequality-finite).
κ > 2 is sharp: for irrational real α, Dirichlet gives infinitely many ξ = p/q with |ξ − α| < q^{−2} ≤ (1 + |α|)²H(ξ)^{−2}, so κ = 2 with C = (1 + |α|)² has infinitely many solutions.

nodes.title: The exponent 1 − n for one linear form is attained (Evertse Lemma 7.6)
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 2 and α_1, …, α_n ∈ ℝ be linearly independent over ℚ. Then there is C > 0 such that |α_1x_1 + ⋯ + α_nx_n| ≤ C‖x‖^{1−n} (7.8) has infinitely many solutions x ∈ ℤ^n; one may take C = |α_n| n^{n−1} after renumbering so that |α_n| = max_i |α_i|.
hypotheses: n ≥ 2; α_1, …, α_n real and linearly independent over ℚ (in particular every α_i ≠ 0)
proofSteps: Renumber so that |α_n| = max_i |α_i| (> 0) and put β_i := −α_i/α_n, so |β_i| ≤ 1 (i < n); write x' = (x_1, …, x_{n−1}).

For each integer Q > 1 apply Minkowski's linear forms theorem (Evertse Corollary 2.6, requested from GeometryOfNumbersAndQuadraticArithmetic:GN.1) to X_1, …, X_{n−1}, X_n − β_1X_1 − ⋯ − β_{n−1}X_{n−1} (determinant 1) with A_1 = ⋯ = A_{n−1} = Q, A_n = Q^{1−n}: there is a non-zero x ∈ ℤ^n with max_{i<n}|x_i| ≤ Q and |x_n − β·x'| ≤ Q^{1−n}.
x' ≠ 0: otherwise |x_n| ≤ Q^{1−n} < 1 forces x = 0. Hence |x_n − β·x'| ≤ Q^{1−n} ≤ max_{i<n}|x_i|^{1−n} (7.9).
α_n(x_n − β·x') = α·x ≠ 0 for x ≠ 0 by linear independence, while |x_n − β·x'| ≤ Q^{1−n} → 0; so as Q → ∞ infinitely many distinct x occur.
From (7.9), |x_n| ≤ 1 + Σ_{i<n}|β_i||x_i| ≤ n max_{i<n}|x_i|, so ‖x‖ ≤ n max_{i<n}|x_i|; inserting and multiplying by |α_n| gives (7.8) with C = |α_n|n^{n−1}.

The source only says that the infinitude of solutions of (7.9) follows 'for instance from Minkowski's convex body theorem'; the second and fourth steps supply that argument (recorded in sourceIssues).
acceptance: Theorem 7.7 shows the exponent 1 − n cannot be lowered to 1 − n − δ when the α_i are algebraic.
n = 2, α = (1, −√2): infinitely many (x_1, x_2) with |x_1 − √2 x_2| ≤ 2√2 ‖x‖^{−1} (Dirichlet).

nodes.title: Small values of one linear form in algebraic numbers (Evertse Theorem 7.7)
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 1, α_1, …, α_n ∈ Q̄ ⊂ ℂ, C > 0 and δ > 0. Then 0 < |α_1x_1 + ⋯ + α_nx_n| ≤ C‖x‖^{1−n−δ} (7.10) has only finitely many solutions x ∈ ℤ^n.
hypotheses: α_i algebraic complex numbers (no independence hypothesis)
The strict inequality 0 < excludes x with α·x = 0
proofSteps: Induction on n. For n = 1: 0 < |α_1x_1| ≤ C|x_1|^{−δ} bounds |x_1|.
n > 1: if all α_i = 0 there are no solutions; renumber so that α_1 ≠ 0. Then the forms α·X, X_2, …, X_n are linearly independent, and (7.10) with |x_i| ≤ ‖x‖ gives |(α·x)x_2 ⋯ x_n| ≤ C‖x‖^{−δ}.
By subspace-theorem-and-its-exceptional-subspaces the solutions lie in finitely many proper subspaces T_1, …, T_t of ℚ^n.

Fix T_i and a non-trivial rational equation a_1x_1 + ⋯ + a_nx_n = 0 vanishing on T_i, say a_n ≠ 0 after renumbering, so x_n = Σ_{j<n} c_jx_j (c_j ∈ ℚ) on T_i. Substituting gives 0 < |β_1x_1 + ⋯ + β_{n−1}x_{n−1}| ≤ C‖x‖^{1−n−δ} ≤ C(max_{j<n}|x_j|)^{2−n−δ} with β_j = α_j + c_jα_n algebraic (x' = (x_1, …, x_{n−1}) ≠ 0 since otherwise x = 0, and max_{j<n}|x_j| ≤ ‖x‖, 1 − n − δ < 2 − n − δ).
By the induction hypothesis (n − 1 variables) there are finitely many x', each determining x ∈ T_i. Sum over i.
acceptance: For n = 2 and α = (1, −α) with α irrational algebraic this gives Roth's theorem: a solution ξ = x/y of |α − ξ| ≤ C H(ξ)^{−κ}, κ = 2 + δ, satisfies 0 < |x − αy| ≤ C max(|x|, |y|)^{−1−δ}.
Sharpness: by linear-form-dirichlet-exponent the exponent 1 − n cannot replace 1 − n − δ.

nodes.title: Approximation of an algebraic number by algebraic numbers of bounded degree (Evertse Theorem 7.8)
nodes.statement: Let α ∈ Q̄ ⊂ ℂ, d ≥ 1, C > 0 and κ > d + 1. Then |ξ − α| ≤ C·H(ξ)^{−κ} (7.11) has only finitely many solutions ξ ∈ Q̄ with deg ξ ≤ d, where H(ξ) is the maximum of the absolute values of the coefficients of the primitive minimal polynomial of ξ (the polynomial F = a_0X^{deg ξ} + ⋯ ∈ ℤ[X], irreducible, with F(ξ) = 0, a_0 > 0 and coprime coefficients; DT.0's naive height).
hypotheses: α ∈ ℂ algebraic; d ≥ 1; C > 0; κ > d + 1
H is the naive height of an algebraic number (DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.0/naive-height-of-algebraic-number), not the absolute Weil height
proofSteps: Write κ = d + 1 + δ. For a solution ξ let F = x_0 + x_1X + ⋯ + x_dX^d be its primitive minimal polynomial (padded with zero coefficients up to degree d), x := (x_0, …, x_d) ∈ ℤ^{d+1}, so H(ξ) = ‖x‖.

Since F(ξ) = 0, the mean value inequality on the segment from ξ to α (norm_image_sub_le_of_norm_deriv_le_segment_01' applied to t ↦ F(ξ + t(α − ξ))) gives |F(α)| ≤ |α − ξ| · max_{0≤t≤1}|F'(ξ + t(α − ξ))|.

Every point of the segment satisfies |ξ + t(α − ξ)| ≤ |α| + |ξ − α| ≤ |α| + C (as |ξ − α| ≤ C H(ξ)^{−κ} ≤ C); hence |F'(ξ + t(α − ξ))| ≤ Σ_{i=1}^d i|x_i|(|α| + C)^{i−1} ≤ C'‖x‖ with C' depending on α, C, d. (The source writes ≤ |α| + |ξ| ≤ |α| + C, whose second step is not justified; see sourceIssues.)

Only finitely many ξ are conjugates of α; for the others F(α) ≠ 0 (F irreducible, F(α) = 0 would make F the minimal polynomial of α up to sign), so 0 < |Σ_i x_iα^i| = |F(α)| ≤ C'‖x‖|ξ − α| ≤ C'C‖x‖^{−d−δ} = C'C‖x‖^{1−(d+1)−δ}.

By single-linear-form-inequality-finite with n = d + 1 and coefficients 1, α, …, α^d there are finitely many x, hence finitely many F, hence finitely many ξ (each F has at most d roots). The source cites 'Theorem 7.8 with n = d + 1', a misprint for Theorem 7.7.
acceptance: d = 1 recovers roth-from-subspace-theorem (κ > 2) for rational approximations.
The source establishes finiteness for κ>d+1; this node makes no assertion of optimality or of a matching infinite-approximation theorem.
Two height conventions: for ξ ∈ ℚ, H(ξ) agrees with max(|x|, |y|) (Mathlib's mulHeight₁ on ℚ); for algebraic ξ of degree > 1 it differs from the absolute Weil height.

nodes.title: Embedding vectors of ℚ-independent elements are independent (Evertse Lemma 7.10)
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field of degree d with complex embeddings σ_1, …, σ_d, and α_1, …, α_n ∈ K linearly independent over ℚ. Then the vectors (σ_1(α_i), …, σ_d(α_i)) ∈ ℂ^d (i = 1, …, n) are linearly independent over ℂ.
hypotheses: K a number field, [K : ℚ] = d
α_1, …, α_n ∈ K linearly independent over ℚ (so n ≤ d)
proofSteps: Extend α_1, …, α_n to a ℚ-basis α_1, …, α_d of K (Module.Basis.extend).

The d × d matrix (σ_i(α_j)) has determinant whose square is the discriminant of the basis (Algebra.discr_eq_det_embeddingsMatrixReindex_pow_two), which is non-zero (Algebra.discr_not_zero_of_basis; K/ℚ is separable). The source argues instead with the Vandermonde matrix of a primitive element; both give det(σ_i(α_j)) ≠ 0.
The columns of an invertible matrix are linearly independent (Matrix.linearIndependent_rows_iff_isUnit applied to the transpose); in particular the first n columns are.
acceptance: Non-example of dropping the hypothesis: α_1 = 1, α_2 = 2 are ℚ-dependent and give proportional vectors.

sources.match: The statement; its proof extends to a basis and uses Vandermonde's identity.

nodes.title: Conjugate linear factors of a norm form are in general position when the Galois group is S_d (Evertse Lemma 7.11)
nodes.statement: Let K = ℚ(θ) be a number field of degree d with embeddings σ_i(θ) = θ^{(i)} (i = 1, …, d), G := ℚ(θ^{(1)}, …, θ^{(d)}) the normal closure, and suppose Gal(G/ℚ) acts on θ^{(1)}, …, θ^{(d)} as the full symmetric group S_d. Let 1 ≤ n ≤ d and α_1, …, α_n ∈ K linearly independent over ℚ. Then the d linear forms L_i := σ_i(α_1)X_1 + ⋯ + σ_i(α_n)X_n (i = 1, …, d) are in general position.
hypotheses: K = ℚ(θ), [K : ℚ] = d
Gal(G/ℚ) ≅ S_d via its action on the conjugates of θ (in Mathlib terms: Polynomial.Gal.galActionHom (minpoly ℚ θ) ℂ is surjective)
α_1, …, α_n ∈ K linearly independent over ℚ
proofSteps: By embedding-vectors-linearly-independent the d × n matrix (σ_i(α_j)) has column rank n, hence row rank n: some n rows i_1, …, i_n are independent, i.e. det(L_{i_1}, …, L_{i_n}) ≠ 0.

Given another n-tuple of distinct indices (j_1, …, j_n), the S_d hypothesis gives τ ∈ Gal(G/ℚ) with τ(θ^{(i_k)}) = θ^{(j_k)}, hence τ∘σ_{i_k} = σ_{j_k}, and τ maps the coefficients of L_{i_k} to those of L_{j_k}.
Therefore det(L_{j_1}, …, L_{j_n}) = τ(det(L_{i_1}, …, L_{i_n})) ≠ 0.
acceptance: K = ℚ(∛2) (d = 3, Galois group S_3), α = (1, ∛2): the three forms X_1 + ρ^i∛2 X_2 (ρ = e^{2πi/3}) are pairwise independent.
Exercise 7.4: for K = ℚ(⁵√2) the Galois group has order 20, the lemma does not apply, but general position still holds for 1, ⁵√2, ⁵√4 (the hypothesis is sufficient, not necessary).

nodes.title: Norm form equations with Galois group S_d have finitely many solutions (Evertse Theorem 7.9)
nodes.statement: Let K = ℚ(θ) be a number field of degree d whose normal closure has Galois group S_d acting on the conjugates of θ, let 1 ≤ n < d and α_1, …, α_n ∈ K linearly independent over ℚ. Then for every c ∈ ℚ the norm form equation N_{K/ℚ}(α_1x_1 + ⋯ + α_nx_n) = c (7.13) has only finitely many solutions x ∈ ℤ^n.
hypotheses: K = ℚ(θ), [K : ℚ] = d, Galois group of the normal closure ≅ S_d
n < d
α_1, …, α_n ∈ K linearly independent over ℚ
c ∈ ℚ (for c = 0 the only solution is x = 0)
proofSteps: Induction on n. n = 1: N_{K/ℚ}(α_1x_1) = N_{K/ℚ}(α_1)x_1^d = c with N(α_1) ≠ 0 has finitely many solutions.

n ≥ 2: F(x) := N_{K/ℚ}(α·x) = ∏_{i=1}^d L_i(x) with L_i = σ_i(α_1)X_1 + ⋯ + σ_i(α_n)X_n (Algebra.norm_eq_prod_embeddings). By norm-form-linear-factors-general-position the L_i are in general position, and d > n.

For c ≠ 0 (for c = 0 only x = 0 solves the equation), subspace-theorem-general-position with r = d, C = |c| and δ := (d − n)/2 applies, since |F(x)| = |c| ≤ |c|·‖x‖^{d−n−δ} for x ≠ 0: the solutions lie in finitely many proper subspaces of ℚ^n.

On such a subspace T, after renumbering, x_n = a_1x_1 + ⋯ + a_{n−1}x_{n−1} with a_i ∈ ℚ; substituting gives N_{K/ℚ}(β_1x_1 + ⋯ + β_{n−1}x_{n−1}) = c with β_i = α_i + a_iα_n, which are linearly independent over ℚ (a relation Σ c_iβ_i = 0 is the relation Σ c_iα_i + (Σ c_ia_i)α_n = 0).
By the induction hypothesis (n − 1 < d variables, same K) there are finitely many (x_1, …, x_{n−1}), each determining x ∈ T.
acceptance: n = d is excluded: for K real quadratic and n = d = 2 (e.g. x² − ay² = 1, the Pell equation) there are infinitely many solutions.
K = ℚ(∛2), d = 3, n = 2, α = (1, ∛2): N(x − ∛2 y) = x³ − 2y³ = c, the Thue equation, has finitely many solutions (Galois group S_3).

nodes.title: The unit group of a number field is infinite unless the field is ℚ or imaginary quadratic
nodes.statement: Let L be a number field with ring of integers O_L. Then O_L^* is infinite if and only if L ≠ ℚ and L is not imaginary quadratic (i.e. not ([L : ℚ] = 2 and L totally complex)); equivalently, iff L has at least two infinite places.
hypotheses: L a number field
proofSteps: By Dirichlet's unit theorem, finrank_ℤ (Additive O_L^*) = rank L = #InfinitePlace(L) − 1 (NumberField.Units.finrank_eq, NumberField.Units.rank).
O_L^* is a finitely generated abelian group, so it is finite iff it is torsion iff its ℤ-finrank is 0 (Module.finrank_eq_zero_iff_isTorsion), iff #InfinitePlace(L) = 1.

#InfinitePlace = r_1 + r_2 and r_1 + 2r_2 = [L : ℚ] (NumberField.InfinitePlace.card_eq_nrRealPlaces_add_nrComplexPlaces, card_add_two_mul_card_eq_rank); r_1 + r_2 = 1 iff (r_1, r_2) = (1, 0), i.e. L = ℚ, or (0, 1), i.e. L imaginary quadratic.
acceptance: L = ℚ(√2): 1 + √2 is a unit of infinite order.
L = ℚ(i): O_L^* = {±1, ±i} is finite.
L = ℚ(∛2): 1 − ∛2 is a unit ((1 − ∛2)(1 + ∛2 + ∛4) = −1) of infinite order.

sources.match: The statement and its derivation from Dirichlet's unit theorem.

nodes.title: Degenerate modules give norm form equations with infinitely many solutions (Evertse Theorem 7.13, (ii) ⇒ (i))
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field, α_1, …, α_n ∈ K linearly independent over ℚ, and M := ℤα_1 + ⋯ + ℤα_n. Suppose there are µ ∈ K^* and a subfield L ⊆ K with L ≠ ℚ and L not imaginary quadratic such that µO_L ⊆ M. Then with c := N_{K/ℚ}(µ) ∈ ℚ^*, the equation N_{K/ℚ}(ξ) = c (7.14) has infinitely many solutions ξ ∈ M; equivalently N_{K/ℚ}(α_1x_1 + ⋯ + α_nx_n) = c has infinitely many solutions x ∈ ℤ^n.
hypotheses: K a number field; α_1, …, α_n ∈ K linearly independent over ℚ; M their ℤ-span (a free ℤ-module of rank n)
µ ∈ K^*, L a subfield of K, L ≠ ℚ, L not imaginary quadratic, µO_L ⊆ M
proofSteps: O_L^* is infinite (unit-group-infinite-criterion). For ε ∈ O_L^*: ε² ∈ O_L, so µε² ∈ µO_L ⊆ M.
N_{K/ℚ}(ε) = N_{L/ℚ}(N_{K/L}(ε)) = N_{L/ℚ}(ε)^{[K:L]} = ±1 (Algebra.norm_norm, NumberField.isUnit_iff_norm), so N_{K/ℚ}(µε²) = N_{K/ℚ}(µ)N_{K/ℚ}(ε)² = c.
ε ↦ ε² has fibres of size ≤ 2 on the infinite group O_L^*, so the elements µε² are infinitely many distinct solutions; since the α_i are independent each ξ ∈ M corresponds to exactly one x ∈ ℤ^n.
acceptance: Example (Evertse p. 150, sign corrected): K = ℚ(⁶√2), M = ℤ⁶√2 + ℤ√2 + ℤ⁶√2⁵ = ⁶√2·ℤ[∛2]; since 1 − ∛2 is a unit of ℤ[∛2] with N_{K/ℚ}(1 − ∛2) = N_{ℚ(∛2)/ℚ}(1 − ∛2)² = 1, every ξ = ⁶√2(1 − ∛2)^k (k ∈ ℤ) lies in M with N_{K/ℚ}(ξ) = N_{K/ℚ}(⁶√2) = −2 (the source prints 2).
Pell: K = L = ℚ(√a) real quadratic, M = O_K: N(ξ) = 1 has infinitely many solutions.

nodes.title: Schmidt's theorem on norm form equations (Evertse Theorem 7.13, (i) ⇒ (ii))
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field, α_1, …, α_n ∈ K linearly independent over ℚ, and M := ℤα_1 + ⋯ + ℤα_n. Suppose (i): there do not exist µ ∈ K^* and a subfield L of K with L ≠ ℚ and L not imaginary quadratic such that µO_L ⊆ M. Then (ii): for every c ∈ ℚ^*, the equation N_{K/ℚ}(ξ) = c in ξ ∈ M has only finitely many solutions. Together with degenerate-module-norm-form-infinitely-many-solutions, (i) and (ii) are equivalent (Schmidt 1972).
hypotheses: K a number field; α_1, …, α_n ∈ K linearly independent over ℚ
Condition (i): M contains no µO_L with L ≠ ℚ, L not imaginary quadratic
c ∈ ℚ^*
proofSteps: The source states that this implication is deduced from the Subspace Theorem and that 'the proof is too difficult to be included here'.

Schmidt's proof (Annals of Math. 96 (1972); Lecture Notes in Math. 785, Chapter VII) applies subspace-theorem-general-position to the d conjugate linear factors of N_{K/ℚ}(α·X) and analyses the exceptional subspaces through the subfields of K; neither source is publicly available and no public full proof was read (recorded as a gap).
The known proofs are ineffective, like the Subspace Theorem.
acceptance: Exercise 7.5(i): K = ℚ(⁶√2), N_{K/ℚ}(x_1 + θx_2 + θ²x_3) = c with θ = ⁶√2 has finitely many solutions for every c ≠ 0 (M contains no µℤ[θ²] or µℤ[θ³]).

Consistency with norm-form-equation-finite-full-symmetric-group: when Gal ≅ S_d and n < d, M cannot contain µO_L for a subfield L ≠ ℚ of degree ≥ 2 (then n ≥ [L : ℚ] and K has no proper subfields other than ℚ when the Galois group is S_d).

nodes.title: p-adic Roth theorem (Ridout; Evertse Theorem 8.6)
nodes.statement: Keep notation (8.4) and let κ > 2, C > 0, and α_p ∈ K for each p ∈ {∞, p_1, …, p_s}. Then |α_∞ − ξ|_∞ · |α_{p_1} − ξ|_{p_1} ⋯ |α_{p_s} − ξ|_{p_s} ≤ C·H(ξ)^{−κ} (8.5) has only finitely many solutions ξ ∈ ℚ, where H(x/y) = max(|x|, |y|).
hypotheses: Notation (8.4): K a number field, continuations |·|_p to K
α_p ∈ K for each p (possibly different)
proofSteps: Let ξ = x/y with gcd(x, y) = 1 and ε := κ − 2. Multiply (8.5) by A := (|y| · |y|_{p_1} ⋯ |y|_{p_s})²; since |y|_{p_j} ≤ 1, A ≤ y² ≤ H(ξ)².
Since |α_p − x/y|_p·|y|_p² = |(x − α_py)y|_p, this gives |(x − α_∞y)y|_∞ ∏_j |(x − α_{p_j}y)y|_{p_j} ≤ C max(|x|, |y|)^{−ε}.
At each p the forms X − α_pY and Y are linearly independent; by p-adic-subspace-theorem the pairs (x, y) lie in finitely many one-dimensional subspaces of ℚ², each giving one fraction x/y.
acceptance: s = 0, α_∞ = α real algebraic: Roth's theorem (roth-from-subspace-theorem).

Example (Evertse (8.6)): for α real irrational algebraic, p prime, ε > 0, C > 0 there are finitely many (u, y) with u > 0, p ∤ y and |α − p^u/y| ≤ C max(p^u, |y|)^{−1−ε}; take α_∞ = α, α_p = 0 (so the p-adic factor |ξ|_p = p^{−u} gains the missing exponent).

nodes.title: A square-free binary form splits into pairwise independent linear factors
nodes.statement: Let F(X, Y) ∈ ℤ[X, Y] be a binary form (homogeneous polynomial) of degree n ≥ 1 which is square-free in ℚ[X, Y]. Then there are β_i, γ_i ∈ Q̄ ⊂ ℂ (i = 1, …, n) with F(X, Y) = ∏_{i=1}^n (β_iX − γ_iY), and the n linear forms β_iX − γ_iY are in general position (pairwise linearly independent). Explicitly, F = a_0∏(X − α_iY) with distinct α_i if F(1, 0) = a_0 ≠ 0, and F = a_0Y∏_{i<n}(X − α_iY) with distinct α_i if F(1, 0) = 0.
hypotheses: F ∈ ℤ[X, Y] homogeneous of degree n ≥ 1
F square-free in ℚ[X, Y] (no repeated irreducible factor; content is irrelevant)
proofSteps: If F(1, 0) = a_0 ≠ 0, f(X) := F(X, 1) has degree n and leading coefficient a_0; f is square-free, hence separable in characteristic 0 (PerfectField.separable_iff_squarefree), hence has n distinct roots α_i ∈ ℂ (Polynomial.nodup_roots, splitting over the algebraically closed ℂ). Homogenising gives F = a_0∏(X − α_iY).
If F(1, 0) = 0 then Y | F; F = Y·G with G(1, 0) ≠ 0 (otherwise Y² | F), and G(X, 1) has degree n − 1 and distinct roots as before.

Absorb a₀ into one factor X−α_iY when there is such a factor. If F=a₀Y has degree1, use the single pair (β,γ)=(0,−a₀) instead, avoiding a nonexistent root α₁. In higher degree retain the factor Y=(0·X−(−1)Y). Distinct roots give independence of X−α_iY and X−α_jY, and Y is independent of each; thus the factors are in general position in two variables.
acceptance: F = XY(X + Y) (degree 3): factors X, Y, X + Y, in general position.
Non-example: F = X²Y is not square-free; its factors X, X, Y are not in general position.

nodes.title: Mahler's theorem on the Thue–Mahler equation (Evertse Theorem 8.10)
nodes.statement: Let F(X, Y) ∈ ℤ[X, Y] be a square-free binary form of degree n ≥ 3 and p_1, …, p_s distinct primes (s ≥ 0). Then the Thue–Mahler equation |F(x, y)| = p_1^{z_1} ⋯ p_s^{z_s} in x, y, z_1, …, z_s ∈ ℤ with gcd(x, y) = 1 (8.10) has only finitely many solutions. The proof via the p-adic Subspace Theorem is ineffective; an effective proof exists via lower bounds for linear forms in complex and p-adic logarithms (DT.4).
hypotheses: F ∈ ℤ[X, Y] homogeneous of degree n ≥ 3, square-free
p_1, …, p_s distinct primes
gcd(x, y) = 1 (without it, scaling produces infinitely many solutions)
proofSteps: By squarefree-binary-form-linear-factors, F = ∏_{i=1}^n (β_iX − γ_iY) with forms in general position; let K := ℚ(β_i, γ_i) and choose continuations |·|_p to K (absolute-value-continuation-exists).

Fix ε with 0 < ε < n − 2. For a solution, F(x, y) = ±∏p_j^{z_j}, so by rational-s-unit-product-criterion |F(x, y)| ∏_j |F(x, y)|_{p_j} = 1 ≤ max(|x|, |y|)^{n−2−ε}, i.e. ∏_{p ∈ {∞, p_1, …, p_s}} |∏_i (β_ix − γ_iy)|_p ≤ ‖(x, y)‖^{n−2−ε}.

By p-adic-subspace-theorem-general-position (two variables, r_p = n forms at each place) the primitive (x, y) lie in finitely many one-dimensional subspaces of ℚ², each containing exactly two primitive points ±(x_0, y_0).
Each (x, y) determines the z_j (F(x, y) ≠ 0 by the equation).

n = 2 fails: x² − 2y² = ±1 (s = 0) has infinitely many coprime solutions.
F = XY(X + Y), S = {2, 3}: coprime solutions of |xy(x + y)| = 2^a3^b include (1, 1), (1, 2), (1, −3), (1, 3), (1, 8), finitely many in total.

nodes.title: Lang's unit equation ax + by = 1 over a finitely generated subgroup of ℚ^* (Evertse Theorem 8.12, case Γ ⊂ ℚ^*)
nodes.statement: Let a, b ∈ ℚ^* and let Γ be a finitely generated subgroup of ℚ^*. Then ax + by = 1 (8.12) has only finitely many solutions x, y ∈ Γ.
hypotheses: a, b ∈ ℚ^*
Γ ⊂ ℚ^* finitely generated (Mathlib Subgroup.FG on ℚˣ)
proofSteps: Choose generators g_1, …, g_r of Γ modulo ±1 and primes p_1, …, p_s containing all primes in the numerators and denominators of a, b, g_1, …, g_r.
For a solution write ax = u/w, by = v/w with u, v, w ∈ ℤ, gcd(u, v, w) = 1, w > 0; then u + v = w, gcd(u, v) = 1, and u, v, w are composed of p_1, …, p_s, so |uv(u + v)| = p_1^{z_1} ⋯ p_s^{z_s}.
F := XY(X + Y) is a square-free binary form of degree 3, so by thue-mahler-finiteness there are finitely many (u, v), hence finitely many (u, v, w) and (x, y).
acceptance: Example (Evertse (8.13)): for Γ generated by 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, x + y = 1 with x ≤ y has exactly 545 solutions (de Weger), e.g. (3/7, 4/7).

nodes.title: Non-degenerate solutions of a linear equation in several unknowns
nodes.statement: Let K be a field, ι a finite index set and α = (α_i)_{i ∈ ι} ∈ (K^*)^ι. A solution x = (x_i) ∈ K^ι of the inhomogeneous equation Σ_{i ∈ ι} α_ix_i = 1 (8.14) is non-degenerate if Σ_{i ∈ I} α_ix_i ≠ 0 for every non-empty subset I ⊆ ι. (For the homogeneous version see nondegenerate-homogeneous-solution.)
hypotheses: K a field; ι finite (Evertse: ι = {1, …, n}, n ≥ 2)
Only non-empty subsets are tested; for I = ι the sum is 1 ≠ 0 automatically
proofSteps: IsNondegenerateSolution α x :⇔ Σ_i α_ix_i = 1 ∧ ∀ I : Finset ι, I.Nonempty → Σ_{i ∈ I} α_ix_i ≠ 0.
acceptance: Every solution with #ι = 1 is non-degenerate.
For 2^u − 2^v + 3^w = 1, the solutions with u = v, w = 0 are degenerate (the subsum 2^u − 2^v vanishes).

Restriction boundary: with α=(1,1,1,1,1) and x=(2,−2,3,−3,1), I={1,2} is a minimal vanishing subset, but its complement is degenerate. Maximality, or the explicit nonvanishing hypothesis used in the suggested signature, is necessary.

nodes.title: Solutions of a homogeneous unit equation over ℚ lie in finitely many proper subspaces (Evertse Lemma 8.15)
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 2, α_0, …, α_n ∈ ℚ^*, Γ ⊂ ℚ^* finitely generated, and H := {x ∈ ℚ^{n+1} : α_0x_0 + ⋯ + α_nx_n = 0}. Then there are finitely many proper linear subspaces T_1, …, T_t of H such that every solution (x_0, …, x_n) ∈ Γ^{n+1} of (8.15), degenerate or not, lies in T_1 ∪ ⋯ ∪ T_t.
hypotheses: n ≥ 2; α_i ∈ ℚ^*; Γ ⊂ ℚ^* finitely generated
Proper subspaces of the n-dimensional space H
proofSteps: Every element of Γ is ±g_1^{u_1} ⋯ g_r^{u_r}; let p_1, …, p_s be the primes dividing the numerators and denominators of α_0, α_1, …, α_n, g_1, …, g_r (the source omits α_0 from this list; it is needed, see sourceIssues). φ : H → ℚ^n, x ↦ (α_1x_1, …, α_nx_n) is a linear bijection.

For a solution x choose w ∈ ℚ_{>0} with y_i := wα_ix_i ∈ ℤ and gcd(y_1, …, y_n) = 1; y = φ(wx) and y_1 + ⋯ + y_n = −wα_0x_0. Then y_1, …, y_n and y_1 + ⋯ + y_n are ± products of p_1, …, p_s, so for 0 < ε < 1, by rational-s-unit-product-criterion, |y_1 ⋯ y_n(y_1 + ⋯ + y_n)| ∏_j |y_1 ⋯ y_n(y_1 + ⋯ + y_n)|_{p_j} = 1 ≤ ‖y‖^{(n+1)−n−ε} (8.16).

The n + 1 forms Y_1, …, Y_n, Y_1 + ⋯ + Y_n are in general position (linear-forms-in-general-position, example inGeneralPosition_coords_add_sum), so p-adic-subspace-theorem-general-position (K = ℚ, r_p = n + 1 at every place) puts the primitive y into finitely many proper subspaces S_1, …, S_t of ℚ^n.
Then x ∈ T_i := φ^{−1}(S_i), a proper subspace of H (w ≠ 0 does not change the subspace).
acceptance: n = 1 is excluded: then H is a line and the only proper subspace is {0}, which contains no solution.
Γ=⟨2⟩ and α=(1,1,−1): all solutions of 2^a+2^b=2^c have a=b and c=a+1. They lie in the line x₀=x₁ inside the two-dimensional hyperplane H.

nodes.title: Every solution has some ratio x_i/x_j in a finite set (Evertse Lemma 8.16)
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 1, α_0, …, α_n ∈ ℚ^* and Γ ⊂ ℚ^* finitely generated. There is a finite set U' ⊂ ℚ^* such that for every solution (x_0, …, x_n) ∈ Γ^{n+1} of α_0x_0 + ⋯ + α_nx_n = 0 (8.15), degenerate or not, there are distinct i, j ∈ {0, …, n} with x_i/x_j ∈ U'.
hypotheses: n ≥ 1; α_i ∈ ℚ^*; Γ ⊂ ℚ^* finitely generated
proofSteps: Induction on n. n = 1: x_0/x_1 = −α_1/α_0.

n ≥ 2: by homogeneous-unit-equation-subspace-cover the solutions lie in proper subspaces T_1, …, T_t of H. Each T satisfies, besides the equation of H, an independent equation γ_0x_0 + ⋯ + γ_nx_n = 0; subtracting (γ_n/α_n) times the first gives β_0x_0 + ⋯ + β_{n−1}x_{n−1} = 0 (8.17) on T with some β_i ≠ 0 (β_i ∈ ℚ).

If exactly one β_i ≠ 0, T contains no solution (x_i ≠ 0). Otherwise apply the induction hypothesis to (8.17) with the vanishing β_i removed (fewer unknowns, coefficients in ℚ^*, unknowns in Γ): a finite set U_T works for the solutions in T.
acceptance: The lemma says nothing about which pair (i, j) occurs; Theorem 8.14 upgrades it to all pairs for non-degenerate solutions.

nodes.title: Ratios of non-degenerate solutions lie in a finite set (Evertse Theorem 8.14)
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 1, α_0, …, α_n ∈ ℚ^* and Γ ⊂ ℚ^* finitely generated. There is a finite set U such that x_i/x_j ∈ U for every non-degenerate solution (x_0, …, x_n) ∈ Γ^{n+1} of α_0x_0 + ⋯ + α_nx_n = 0 (8.15) and every pair of indices i, j ∈ {0, …, n}.
hypotheses: n ≥ 1; α_i ∈ ℚ^*; Γ ⊂ ℚ^* finitely generated
Non-degenerate in the sense of nondegenerate-homogeneous-solution
proofSteps: Induction on n; n = 1 is trivial (x_0/x_1 = −α_1/α_0).
n ≥ 2: let U' = {β_1, …, β_m} be as in homogeneous-unit-equation-ratio-lemma; the non-degenerate solutions split into the finitely many sets S_{pqr} = {x : x_p/x_q = β_r} (p ≠ q).

On S_{pqr}, say p = n, q = n − 1: x_n = β_rx_{n−1}, so α_0x_0 + ⋯ + α_{n−2}x_{n−2} + (α_{n−1} + β_rα_n)x_{n−1} = 0; by non-degeneracy of x the new coefficient α_{n−1} + β_rα_n is non-zero and every proper non-empty subsum is non-zero (nondegenerate-homogeneous-solution, merge).
The induction hypothesis gives a finite set containing x_i/x_j for i, j ≤ n − 1; enlarge it by multiplying with β_r^{±1} to cover pairs involving n. U := union over (p, q, r).
acceptance: Taking α_0 = −1 and x_0 = 1 gives s-unit-equation-over-rationals.
Degenerate solutions are genuinely excluded: for Γ = ⟨2⟩, 2^u − 2^u + 1 = 1 has ratios 2^u unbounded.

nodes.title: Specialisation of finitely many elements of a field to Q̄ (Evertse–Schlickewei–Schmidt Lemma 3.1)
nodes.statement: Let K be an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0 containing Q̄, and U = {u_1, …, u_k} a finite subset of K. Then there is a ring homomorphism φ : Q̄[U] → Q̄ whose restriction to Q̄ is the identity. Consequently every non-zero element of Q̄[U] whose inverse lies in Q̄[U] is mapped to a non-zero element.
hypotheses: K algebraically closed of characteristic 0 with Q̄ ⊆ K (any field of characteristic 0 embeds in such a K)
U finite
proofSteps: Let J ⊂ Q̄[X_1, …, X_k] be the kernel of X_i ↦ u_i; 1 ∉ J, so J is a proper ideal.

By Hilbert's Nullstellensatz over the algebraically closed field Q̄ (MvPolynomial.vanishingIdeal_zeroLocus_eq_radical), J has a zero c ∈ Q̄^k: otherwise the vanishing ideal of its (empty) zero locus, the whole ring, would equal the radical of J, forcing 1 ∈ J.
Then g(u_1, …, u_k) ↦ g mod J ↦ g(c) is a well-defined ring homomorphism Q̄[U] ≅ Q̄[X]/J → Q̄ fixing Q̄. Units map to units, hence to non-zero elements.
acceptance: If U ⊂ Q̄ then φ is the identity on Q̄[U] = Q̄.
U = {π} ⊂ ℂ: φ(π) can be any algebraic number, e.g. 0; so only elements inverted in Q̄[U] are guaranteed to stay non-zero.

nodes.title: Solutions of y_1 + ⋯ + y_n = 1 in a group of finite rank lie in few subspaces (Evertse–Schlickewei–Schmidt Theorem 2.1)
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 2 and let Γ be a subgroup of (Q̄^*)^n of finite rank r. Then the set of y ∈ Q̄^n with y_1 + ⋯ + y_n = 1 (2.6) of the form y = x ∗ z with x ∈ Γ, z ∈ (Q̄^*)^n and h(z) ≤ n^{−1}exp(−(4n)^{3n})(1 + h(x)) (2.10) is contained in the union of at most B(n, r) = exp((5n)^{3n}(r + 1)) proper linear subspaces of Q̄^n. Here ∗ is coordinatewise multiplication and h(x) = log H(x) with H(x) = ∏_v max(1, ‖x_1‖_v, …, ‖x_n‖_v) the absolute multiplicative height.
hypotheses: Γ ⊆ (Q̄^*)^n of finite rank r (not necessarily finitely generated)
h is the absolute logarithmic Weil height (Mathlib: logHeight over a number field containing the coordinates, normalised by the degree)
proofSteps: Proved in ESS §§6–12: §6 reduces to Proposition 6.2; §7 heights in multiplicative groups; §8 special points; §9 properties of large special solutions; §10 large solutions via the quantitative Parametric Subspace Theorem for twisted heights with the special forms X_1, …, X_n, X_1 + ⋯ + X_n (Evertse–Schlickewei 2002, Theorem 2.1, improved by parametric-subspace-theorem, EF Theorem 1.1); §11 small solutions via a gap principle; §12 proof of Proposition 6.2.
These sections are not decomposed here (recorded as a gap); the node's only external input is parametric-subspace-theorem in the special case (1.5)–(1.6) of EF.
acceptance: With z = (1, …, 1) the theorem covers all solutions y ∈ Γ of y_1 + ⋯ + y_n = 1, which is how it enters uniform-bound-nondegenerate-solutions.
The bound depends only on n and r, not on Γ or the field.

nodes.title: Uniform bound for non-degenerate solutions in a group of finite rank (Evertse–Schlickewei–Schmidt Theorem 1.1)
nodes.statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, n ≥ 1, Γ a subgroup of (K^*)^n of finite rank r, and a = (a_1, …, a_n) ∈ (K^*)^n. Then a_1x_1 + ⋯ + a_nx_n = 1 (1.1) has at most A(n, r) = exp((6n)^{3n}(r + 1)) non-degenerate solutions x ∈ Γ.
hypotheses: K of characteristic 0 (the source takes K algebraically closed; any K embeds in its algebraic closure without changing the solution set)
Γ ⊆ (K^*)^n of finite rank r: some finitely generated Γ_0 ⊆ Γ of rank r has Γ/Γ_0 torsion
Non-degenerate: no non-empty subsum vanishes
proofSteps: Reduction to K = Q̄ (ESS Lemma 3.2): it suffices to bound any finite set M = {x_1, …, x_m} of non-degenerate solutions. Apply specialization-to-algebraic-numbers to the finite set U of the a_j, the coordinates x_{ij}, all subsums Σ_{j∈I}a_jx_{ij}, all differences x_{i_1,j} − x_{i_2,j}, and the inverses of the non-zero ones. The images x'_i are distinct non-degenerate solutions of Σ φ(a_j)y_j = 1 in the image of the group generated by M, which has rank ≤ r (nondegenerate-solution, map).

Case K = Q̄ (ESS §4), induction on n (n = 1 trivial): with Γ' generated by a and Γ (rank ≤ r + 1), unit-equation-subspace-bound-algebraic (z = 1) puts all solutions into B(n, r + 1) proper subspaces. On a subspace Σ_{i∈I} b_ix_i = 0 (#I ≥ 2), for each J ⊆ I with Σ_{i∈J} b_ix_i = 0 minimal, write w_i = x_i/x_1 (i ∈ J) and split Γ → Γ_1 (ratios) with kernel Γ_2, ranks r_1 + r_2 = r; induction bounds the (w_i) by A(#J − 1, r_1) and the remaining equation b'x' + Σ_{i∉J} a'_ix'_i = 1 in Γ_2-cosets by A(n − #J + 1, r_2).
Combine: at most 2^n A(n − 1, r) solutions per subspace, and 2^n A(n − 1, r) B(n, r + 1) < A(n, r).
acceptance: n = 1: at most one solution.
Non-degeneracy is necessary: x_1 − x_2 + x_3 = 1 has infinitely many degenerate solutions with x_1 = x_2 in any infinite Γ.

nodes.title: The S-unit equation theorem: finitely many non-degenerate solutions (Evertse Theorems 8.12 and 8.13; van der Poorten–Schlickewei, Evertse, Laurent)
nodes.statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, Γ a finitely generated subgroup of K^*, n ≥ 1 and α_1, …, α_n ∈ K^*. Then α_1x_1 + ⋯ + α_nx_n = 1 (8.14) has only finitely many non-degenerate solutions (x_1, …, x_n) ∈ Γ^n. For n = 2 every solution with x, y ∈ Γ is non-degenerate, so ax + by = 1 has finitely many solutions (Lang's theorem, Evertse 8.12). The known proofs for n ≥ 3 are ineffective; for n = 2 and K a number field an effective proof exists (DT.4).
hypotheses: K of characteristic 0 (any, not only number fields)
Γ ⊆ K^* finitely generated
α_i ∈ K^*
Non-degenerate in the sense of nondegenerate-solution
proofSteps: Γ^n ⊆ (K^*)^n is finitely generated, of finite rank r ≤ n·rank(Γ).
By uniform-bound-nondegenerate-solutions the equation has at most A(n, r) non-degenerate solutions in Γ^n; in particular finitely many.
For n = 2, a solution of ax + by = 1 with x, y ∈ Γ has ax ≠ 0 and by ≠ 0, so it is non-degenerate.
Over ℚ the source proves the case Γ ⊂ ℚ^* directly (s-unit-equation-over-rationals); it agrees with this node.
acceptance: K = ℚ: consistent with s-unit-equation-over-rationals.
DT.2 acceptance: finiteness is separate from effectivity; the bound A(n, r) counts solutions but does not locate them.

nodes.title: Non-degenerate linear recurrences
nodes.statement: A linear recurrence E over ℂ (Mathlib's `LinearRecurrence ℂ`: an order k and coefficients (E.coeffs i)_{i<k}, with solutions u satisfying u(h + k) = Σ_{i<k} E.coeffs i · u(h + i)) is non-degenerate if its characteristic polynomial E.charPoly = X^k − Σ_{i<k} E.coeffs i X^i has non-zero constant term (so all its roots are non-zero; Evertse's c_k ≠ 0) and for any two distinct roots θ ≠ θ' of E.charPoly, the quotient θ/θ' is not a root of unity (¬ IsOfFinOrder (θ/θ')). A linear recurrence sequence is non-degenerate if its minimal recurrence is; a sequence satisfying some non-degenerate recurrence is non-degenerate, since the characteristic polynomial of the minimal recurrence divides that of any recurrence it satisfies.
hypotheses: E : LinearRecurrence ℂ
Evertse's u_h = c_1u_{h−1} + ⋯ + c_ku_{h−k} corresponds to E.coeffs i = c_{k−i}; his companion polynomial f_U is E.charPoly
proofSteps: IsNondegenerate E :⇔ E.charPoly.coeff 0 ≠ 0 ∧ ∀ θ ∈ E.charPoly.roots, ∀ θ' ∈ E.charPoly.roots, θ ≠ θ' → ¬ IsOfFinOrder (θ / θ').
acceptance: Fibonacci u_{h+2} = u_{h+1} + u_h: roots (1 ± √5)/2 with ratio −(3 + √5)/2, of absolute value ≠ 1, hence not a root of unity: non-degenerate.
u_{h+2} = −u_h: roots ±i with ratio −1, a root of unity: degenerate (and u = (0, 1, 0, −1, …) has infinitely many zeros).

uniform bound for zeros of simple non-degenerate recurrences

nodes.title: Skolem–Mahler–Lech for simple roots via the S-unit equation (Evertse Theorem 8.18, case e_i = 1)
nodes.statement: Let m ≥ 1, θ_1, …, θ_m non-zero complex numbers such that no quotient θ_i/θ_j (i ≠ j) is a root of unity, and g_1, …, g_m ∈ ℂ not all 0. Then g_1θ_1^h + ⋯ + g_mθ_m^h = 0 has only finitely many solutions h ∈ ℤ_{≥0}. Equivalently: a non-zero linear recurrence sequence U over ℂ satisfying a non-degenerate recurrence whose characteristic polynomial has no multiple roots has a finite zero set Z_U = {h ≥ 0 : u_h = 0}.
hypotheses: θ_i ∈ ℂ^*, θ_i/θ_j not a root of unity for i ≠ j (in particular the θ_i are distinct)
g_i ∈ ℂ constants, not all zero (U ≠ 0; the source's first formulation omits this, see sourceIssues)
Simple roots only: the general case with polynomial coefficients g_i(h) is proved by p-adic analysis and is not an S-unit application
proofSteps: Discard the indices with g_i = 0 (the hypothesis persists); induction on the number m of remaining terms. m = 1: g_1θ_1^h ≠ 0.
m ≥ 2: put a_i := −g_i/g_m ∈ ℂ^* and β_i := θ_i/θ_m (i < m); the equation becomes a_1β_1^h + ⋯ + a_{m−1}β_{m−1}^h = 1 (8.21), and no β_i and no β_i/β_j (i ≠ j) is a root of unity.

Apply s-unit-equation-finiteness with K = ℂ, Γ generated by β_1, …, β_{m−1}: finitely many non-degenerate solutions (β_1^h, …, β_{m−1}^h); since β_1 is not a root of unity, h ↦ β_1^h is injective, so finitely many h give non-degenerate solutions.

For the other h some subsum Σ_{i∈I} a_iβ_i^h vanishes with ∅ ≠ I ⊆ {1, …, m − 1} (the source writes {1, …, m}); multiplying by θ_m^h, Σ_{i∈I} g_iθ_i^h = 0, an equation with fewer terms satisfying the hypotheses, so the induction hypothesis leaves finitely many h for each of the finitely many I.
Recurrence form: if E has simple roots θ_1, …, θ_k, every solution is u_h = Σ g_iθ_i^h (the closed form requested from ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.2), and u ≠ 0 means some g_i ≠ 0.
acceptance: u_h = 2^h + 3^h − 5^h (Evertse’s example, roots 2, 3, 5, non-degenerate): u_0 = 1, u_1 = 0 and u_h < 0 for h ≥ 2, so the zero set is {1}.
Degenerate counterexample: u_h = i^h + (−i)^h vanishes for all odd h (roots with ratio −1).
Zero sequence: excluded by 'not all g_i zero'.

nodes.title: Uniform bound for the zeros of simple linear recurrences (Evertse–Schlickewei–Schmidt Theorem 1.2)
nodes.statement: Let K be an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0, n ≥ 3, and let u_m = a_1α_1^m + ⋯ + a_nα_n^m (m ∈ ℤ) with a_i ∈ K^* and pairwise distinct α_i ∈ K^* (a simple linear recurrence sequence of order n, indexed by ℤ). Then there are integers k_1, …, k_{q_1} and arithmetic progressions T_i = {a'_i + tv_i : t ∈ ℤ} (v_i ≠ 0, i = 1, …, q_2) with q_1 + q_2 ≤ exp((6n)^{3n}) such that S(u) := {k ∈ ℤ : u_k = 0} = {k_1, …, k_{q_1}} ∪ T_1 ∪ ⋯ ∪ T_{q_2}. If moreover no α_i/α_j (i ≠ j) is a root of unity, then #S(u) ≤ exp((6n)^{3n}).
hypotheses: K algebraically closed of characteristic 0 (any field of characteristic 0 embeds in one)
n ≥ 3 (for n = 2 the zero set is empty or one point, or, in the degenerate case, a union of progressions)
Simple: distinct roots, constant coefficients a_i ≠ 0
proofSteps: Induction on n, with W(n) := exp((6n)^{3n}) and single integers counted as progressions of difference 0 (ESS §5).

Zeros k for which no proper subsum of Σ a_iα_i^k vanishes give non-degenerate solutions ((α_1/α_n)^k, …, (α_{n−1}/α_n)^k) of Σ_{i<n}(−a_i/a_n)x_i = 1 in the rank-≤1 group generated by (α_1/α_n, …, α_{n−1}/α_n); by uniform-bound-nondegenerate-solutions there are at most A(n − 1, 1) such solutions, and each determines an arithmetic progression of k.

Zeros with a vanishing proper subsum Σ_{i∈I} a_iα_i^k = 0 (2 ≤ #I ≤ n − 2) also satisfy Σ_{i∉I} a_iα_i^k = 0; by induction each set is a union of at most W(#I), resp. W(n − #I), progressions, and intersections of progressions are progressions: at most 2^n W(n − 1) progressions in total.

Non-degenerate case: if S(u) contained {a + vt} with v ≠ 0, the Vandermonde determinant det(α_i^{vt})_{i, t<n} would vanish, forcing α_i^v = α_j^v for some i ≠ j, contradicting non-degeneracy; so S(u) is a finite union of at most W(n) points.
acceptance: Quantitative form of skolem-mahler-lech-simple-roots: the bound depends only on the order n.

Degenerate example: u_m = 1 + (−1)^m (roots 1, −1, ratio −1) vanishes exactly on the odd integers, one arithmetic progression; the theorem bounds the number of progressions (here n = 2, below the theorem's range, where the bound is immediate).
Theorem 8.19 of Evertse (Schmidt 2000) extends the non-degenerate bound to non-simple recurrences with a triply exponential bound; not proved in the sources read.

nodes.title: Twisted height H_{L,c,Q} (Evertse–Ferretti (2.13)–(2.15))
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field with normalised absolute values ‖·‖_v (v ∈ M_K), n ≥ 1, L = (L_i^{(v)}) a tuple of linear forms in K[X_1, …, X_n] satisfying (2.5)–(2.6) and c = (c_{iv}) a tuple of reals satisfying (2.7) (for the theorems also (2.8)–(2.9)). For a real Q ≥ 1 the twisted height is H_{L,c,Q}(x) := ∏_{v ∈ M_K} max_{1≤i≤n} (‖L_i^{(v)}(x)‖_v · Q^{−c_{iv}}) for x ∈ K^n. For x ∈ Q̄^n choose a finite extension E ⊇ K with x ∈ E^n and put L_i^{(w)} := L_i^{(v)}, c_{iw} := d(w|v)c_{iv} for w | v, d(w|v) := [E_w : K_v]/[E : K], and H_{L,c,Q}(x) := ∏_{w ∈ M_E} max_i ‖L_i^{(w)}(x)‖_w Q^{−c_{iw}}; this does not depend on E. H_{L,c,Q}(0) = 0; for x ≠ 0 all factors are non-zero and almost all equal 1. With L_i^{(v)} = X_i and c = 0 it is the absolute multiplicative height H(x) = ∏_v max_i ‖x_i‖_v.
hypotheses: K a number field; normalised absolute values with the product formula
(2.5)–(2.7) (and (2.8)–(2.9) as normalisations used by the theorems)
Q ≥ 1 real
proofSteps: Define the local factor at v as max_i ‖L_i^{(v)}(x)‖_v Q^{−c_{iv}} and take the product over v; by (2.5)–(2.7) and x ≠ 0 only finitely many factors differ from 1 (for almost all v the forms are v-integral with unit determinant and c_{iv} = 0, so the factor is ‖x‖_v, which is 1 for almost all v), so the product is a finite product (a finprod over the places).
Independence of E: by d(w|v) summing to 1 over w | v (EF (2.3)) and ‖x‖_w = ‖x‖_v^{d(w|v)} for x ∈ K (EF (2.2)).

Projective invariance H(αx) = H(x) (α ≠ 0) follows from the product formula; Galois invariance H(σx) = H(x) for σ ∈ Gal(Q̄/K) (EF Lemma 4.1) from the fact that σ permutes the places above each v preserving local degrees.
acceptance: c = 0, L = coordinates: H_{L,0,Q}(x) = H(x), the absolute height (for K = ℚ and primitive x ∈ ℤ^n, max_i |x_i|).

nodes.title: Successive infima λ_i(Q) of a twisted height and their subspaces (Evertse–Ferretti §9)
nodes.statement: In the setting of twisted-height, for Q ≥ 1 and λ ≥ 0 let T(Q, λ) be the Q̄-vector space spanned by {x ∈ Q̄^n : H_{L,c,Q}(x) ≤ λ}. The successive infima are λ_i(Q) := inf{λ ≥ 0 : dim T(Q, λ) ≥ i} (i = 1, …, n), and T_i(Q) := ∩_{λ > λ_i(Q)} T(Q, λ). Over Q̄ the infima need not be attained. The spaces T_i(Q) are defined over K (Galois invariance of the twisted height), and if λ_k(Q) < λ_{k+1}(Q) then dim T_k(Q) = k and T(Q, λ) = T_k(Q) for λ_k(Q) < λ < λ_{k+1}(Q) (EF Lemma 9.1).
hypotheses: Setting of twisted-height with (2.4)–(2.7)

Points range over Q̄^n (all finite extensions of K); the Lean prototype uses K-rational points, and the absolute version is the infimum over finite extensions E ⊇ K of the E-rational versions with the lifted data (2.14)
proofSteps: λ_i(Q) is an infimum of a non-empty set of reals bounded below by 0 (T(Q, λ) = Q̄^n for large λ, since H_{L,c,Q}(e_j) < ∞).
EF Lemma 9.1: (i) T(Q, λ) is Gal(Q̄/K)-stable by EF Lemma 4.1, hence defined over K; (ii) dim T(Q, λ) = k for λ_k < λ < λ_{k+1} since dimension jumps exactly at the infima and T(Q, λ) grows with λ.
acceptance: For c = 0 and L = coordinates, λ_i(Q) are the successive minima of the absolute height, λ_1 = ⋯ = λ_n = 1.
