nodes.title: D-finite (holonomic) power series
nodes.statement: Let k ⊆ ℂ be a subfield. A formal power series f ∈ ℂ[[z]] is D-finite over k if there are n ∈ ℕ and polynomials p₀, …, p_n ∈ k[z] with p_n ≠ 0 and Σ_{i=0}^{n} p_i(z)·f^{(i)} = 0, where f^{(i)} is the i-th formal derivative. Equivalently, the k(z)-span of f, f′, f″, … is finite-dimensional; equivalently (when the coefficients of f lie in k) the coefficient sequence is P-recursive: Σ_{i=0}^{r} q_i(n)·c_{n+i} = 0 for all n with q_i ∈ k[X], q_r ≠ 0.
hypotheses: k is a subfield of ℂ (in DT.5 always ℚ, Q̄ = algebraicClosure ℚ ℂ, or ℂ)
The equation is over k[z]; clearing denominators, this is the same as an equation over k(z)
proofSteps: Existential definition over polynomial coefficient tuples indexed by Fin (n + 1), with nonzero leading coefficient.

Closure under +, ×, derivative: the k(z)-spans of derivatives of f + g and fg lie in the span generated by products of derivatives, which is finite-dimensional (Beukers, AWS notes, proof of Proposition 3.2.1).
P-recursiveness: compare coefficients of z^m in Σ p_i f^{(i)} = 0.
acceptance: exp satisfies f′ − f = 0 over ℚ.
1/(1 − z) satisfies (1 − z)f′ − f = 0.
Σ z^{2^n} is not D-finite (it has the unit circle as natural boundary, while a D-finite series with finite radius has finitely many singularities).

nodes.title: The minimal differential equation of a D-finite series
nodes.statement: For a D-finite f over k, its minimal order ord_k(f) is the least n for which an equation Σ_{i=0}^{n} p_i f^{(i)} = 0 with p_i ∈ k[z], p_n ≠ 0 exists (dfiniteOrder). The minimal equations are unique up to a common rational factor: two minimal equations p, p′ satisfy p′_n p_i = p_n p′_i for all i; the monic minimal operator L = ∂^n + Σ_{i<n} (p_i/p_n) ∂^i is Beukers' 'minimal differential equation of f'. A point ξ ∈ ℂ is a singular point of L if the leading coefficient of every minimal equation vanishes at ξ (IsMinimalSingularPoint); a singular point ξ is apparent if L has a basis of solutions holomorphic at ξ.
hypotheses: The apparent-singularity notion uses the local solution space of L at ξ (holomorphic-solutions-of-linear-systems); it has no Lean statement until that API exists
Order 0 occurs only for f = 0
proofSteps: dfiniteOrder := Nat.find of the D-finiteness witness.
Uniqueness: if p, p′ are minimal, p′_n·(Σ p_i ∂^i) − p_n·(Σ p′_i ∂^i) annihilates f and has order < n, so all its coefficients vanish.
Singular points: a pole of some p_i/p_n; independent of the minimal equation chosen by uniqueness.
acceptance: exp: order 1, equation f′ − f = 0, no finite singular point.
(z − 1)eᶻ: order 1, minimal equation (z − 1)f′ = zf, singular (and apparent) at z = 1.
z: order 1 (z f′ − f = 0), singular at 0.

Field-sensitivity test: f = exp(√2 z) has minimal order 2 over ℚ and order 1 over ℚ(√2). The complex-coefficient order-2 operators D²−2 and D²−√2 D both annihilate f but are not proportional; they cannot be compared using minimality over ℚ.

nodes.title: E-functions
nodes.statement: A sequence a : ℕ → ℂ (the power series f(z) = Σ a_n zⁿ/n!) is an E-function if (i) every a_n is algebraic over ℚ; (ii) f is D-finite over Q̄; (iii) there is C > 0 with |σ(a_n)| ≤ C^{n+1} for every conjugate σ(a_n) (every root of the minimal polynomial of a_n); (iv) there are D > 0 and positive integers d_n ≤ D^{n+1} such that d_n a_m is an algebraic integer for all m ≤ n. The function eFun a : ℂ → ℂ, z ↦ Σ a_n zⁿ/n!, is entire. This is the geometric normalisation of Shidlovskii, André, Beukers and Fischler–Rivoal; Siegel's original definition allowed growth (n!)^ε and is not used.
hypotheses: The coefficients then lie in a single number field (the differential equation has finitely many algebraic coefficients)
Conventions: an E-function is recorded by its coefficient sequence a with the factorials divided out; the power series is ePowerSeries a
proofSteps: Structure with four fields as in the statement; ePowerSeries, eFun and the Hurwitz product hurwitzMul are auxiliary definitions.

Ring structure: (a + b) and the binomial convolution hurwitzMul a b satisfy (iii) with 2C and (iv) with D² (AWS Proposition 3.2.1, promoted to e-functions-form-a-ring); the shift a(n + 1) (derivative) satisfies the bounds with a larger constant.
Conjugates: applying a ring automorphism of ℂ to the coefficients preserves (i)–(iv) (conjugate differential equation, same minimal polynomials).
acceptance: exp (a_n=1), the explicitly normalised Bessel-type series ∑ z^(2k)/(k!)² (a_(2k)=binom(2k,k), a_(2k+1)=0), and pFq[a;b;z^(q−p+1)] with q≥p≥1, rational upper parameters and rational lower parameters outside ℤ≤0 are E-functions. The AWS symbol J₀(−z²) denotes that displayed series; do not interpret it using the standard argument normalisation J₀(w)=∑(iw/2)^(2k)/(k!)².
(z − 1)eᶻ has a_n = n − 1.

sources.match: Conditions (i)–(ii); (iii) is the denominator bound d_n ≤ D^{n+1}.
The same definition with |a_n| the size (maximum of the conjugates).

nodes.title: G-functions
nodes.statement: A sequence a : ℕ → ℂ (the power series Σ a_n zⁿ) is a G-function if its coefficients are algebraic, Σ a_n zⁿ is D-finite over Q̄, all conjugates satisfy |σ(a_n)| ≤ C^{n+1}, and there are positive integers d_n ≤ D^{n+1} with d_n a_m integral for m ≤ n. Equivalently (Fischler–Rivoal), Σ a_n zⁿ is a G-function iff Σ a_n zⁿ/n! is an E-function. G-functions have a positive radius of convergence.

nodes.title: Mahler functions
nodes.statement: Let q ≥ 2 be an integer. A power series f ∈ ℂ[[z]] with algebraic coefficients is q-Mahler if there are polynomials p₀, …, p_n ∈ Q̄[z], not all zero, with p₀(z)f(z) + p₁(z)f(z^q) + ⋯ + p_n(z)f(z^{qⁿ}) = 0. Equivalently, f is a coordinate of a solution F = (f₁, …, f_m) of a Mahler system F(z) = A(z)F(z^q), A ∈ GL_m(Q̄(z)). The series f(z^r) is expandPow r f.
hypotheses: Coefficients algebraic (AF work with f ∈ Q̄{z}, convergent near 0)
q ≥ 2 is part of the data; the relation is over Q̄[z]
proofSteps: Existential definition as stated; expandPow r f has coefficient c_{m/r} at m when r ∣ m and 0 otherwise.
Ring structure: the Q̄(z)-span of {f(z^{q^i})} is finite-dimensional and stable under z ↦ z^q; products of two such spans are again finite-dimensional.
System form: take F = (f(z), f(z^q), …, f(z^{q^{n−1}})) and the companion matrix of the relation (after reducing to p₀p_n ≠ 0).
acceptance: Σ z^{2^n} is 2-Mahler: z f(z) − (1 + z) f(z²) + f(z⁴) = 0.
The Thue–Morse product ∏(1 − z^{2^n}) satisfies f(z) = (1 − z) f(z²).

nodes.title: Regular points of a Mahler system
nodes.statement: Let q ≥ 2 and A ∈ GL_n(ℂ(z)) (a Mahler system F(z) = A(z)F(z^q)). A point α with 0 < |α| < 1 is regular if for no ℓ ≥ 0 is α^{q^ℓ} a pole of an entry of A or of A⁻¹ (with rational functions in lowest terms, poles are zeros of the denominator RatFunc.denom). Otherwise α is a singularity; the singularities have no accumulation point in the open unit disc.

α regular ⇒ α^q regular (shift ℓ).
Polynomial A with constant nonzero determinant: A and A⁻¹ have no poles, so every α with 0 < |α| < 1 is regular.

nodes.title: Schanuel's conjecture (as an explicit hypothesis)
nodes.statement: SchanuelConjecture is the proposition: for every n and every z₁, …, z_n ∈ ℂ linearly independent over ℚ, the transcendence degree over ℚ of ℚ(z₁, …, z_n, e^{z₁}, …, e^{z_n}) is at least n. It is a statement, not an assumption of the library: every consequence in DT.5 takes it as a hypothesis.

proofSteps: Definition of the proposition with its complete body.
Unconditional instances: for algebraic z_i it is the Lindemann–Weierstrass theorem (DT.3), recorded as the API item schanuel_inequality_of_isAlgebraic; for n = 1 it is Hermite–Lindemann.
acceptance: The consequences algebraicIndependent_e_pi_of_schanuel and logarithmsConjecture_of_schanuel are proved from it.

nodes.title: Cauchy's theorem for linear differential systems
nodes.statement: Let r > 0 and A = (A_ij) be an n × n matrix of functions holomorphic on the disc D = {z : |z−z₀|<r}. For every initial vector y₀ ∈ ℂⁿ there exists a vector y of functions holomorphic on D with y(z₀)=y₀ and y′=Ay on D. Any two such solutions agree on D. If represented by total functions ℂ→ℂ, uniqueness is equality on D, not equality of their unconstrained values outside D.
hypotheses: Coefficients holomorphic on the whole disc (for A ∈ M_n(ℂ(z)): the disc avoids the poles)
Uniqueness uses the identity theorem on the connected disc
r > 0, so the initial point is in the domain. Equality of solutions means agreement on the disc (or equality of restricted-domain solutions).
proofSteps: Write A = Σ A_k (z − z₀)^k and look for y = Σ y_k (z − z₀)^k: (k + 1)y_{k+1} = Σ_{j≤k} A_{k−j} y_j determines the y_k recursively.
Majorants: for ρ < r, ‖A_k‖ ≤ M ρ^{−k}; the scalar series solving u′ = M(1 − (z − z₀)/ρ)^{−1}u with u(z₀) = ‖y₀‖ dominates the y_k and converges on |z − z₀| < ρ; let ρ → r.
Uniqueness: the difference of two solutions with the same initial value has all Taylor coefficients zero at z₀, hence vanishes on the disc (identity theorem).
acceptance: y′ = y on ℂ: solutions c·eᶻ, a one-dimensional space.
(z − 1)y′ = zy on |z| < 1: the solution with y(0) = −1 is (z − 1)eᶻ; on a disc around 1 the coefficient z/(z − 1) is not holomorphic and the theorem does not apply (the singularity is apparent).
Changing a total representative outside D does not produce a different solution on D. Global-function uniqueness would be false even for y′=0.

sources.match: The local existence theorem at a regular point (the source adds convergence when the coefficients converge); the node states it on the whole disc of holomorphy of the coefficients. The theorem is stated on a positive-radius disc with uniqueness on that disc. The source is local; extension to the entire pole-free disc uses the majorant argument. Solution-space and scalar-equation consequences are now separate nodes.

nodes.title: Kähler differentials of a field extension and transcendence degree
nodes.statement: Let E/C be a finitely generated field extension of characteristic 0. Then dim_E Ω_{E/C} = trdeg_C E, and for every transcendence basis x₁, …, x_t of E/C the differentials dx₁, …, dx_t form an E-basis of Ω_{E/C}.
hypotheses: Characteristic 0 (so every transcendence basis is separating)
Finitely generated as a field (Algebra.EssFiniteType)
proofSteps: Choose a transcendence basis x (exists_isTranscendenceBasis); E/C(x) is finite and separable (char 0: Algebra.IsAlgebraic.isSeparable_of_perfectField).
Ω_{C[x]/C} is free on dx_i (KaehlerDifferential.mvPolynomialBasis) and localises to Ω_{C(x)/C} (KaehlerDifferential.isLocalizedModule).
E/C(x) is formally étale (Algebra.FormallyEtale.of_isSeparable), so E ⊗_{C(x)} Ω_{C(x)/C} ≃ Ω_{E/C} (KaehlerDifferential.tensorKaehlerEquivOfFormallyEtale), sending 1 ⊗ dx_i to dx_i.
acceptance: E = C(t): Ω is one-dimensional with basis dt (compatibility with tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/AlgebraicCurves layer 9, 'Ω[F⁄k] is one-dimensional', the transcendence-degree-one case).
E = C(t, eᵗ)-type fields with trdeg 2 have two-dimensional Ω.

sources.match: The fact used in the proof of Ax's theorem, planned here in general.

nodes.title: Fibres of a torsion-free family over the affine line
nodes.statement: Let K be a field and A a finitely generated K[z]-algebra which is a domain and torsion-free over K[z]. For ξ ∈ K with A/(z − ξ)A ≠ 0: dim A/(z − ξ)A = dim A − 1, and dim A = trdeg_K Frac(A) = 1 + trdeg_{K(z)} Frac(A). In particular, if A/(z − ξ)A is a domain its fraction field has transcendence degree trdeg_{K(z)} Frac(A) over K.
hypotheses: Torsion-free over the PID K[z] (equivalently flat)
Krull dimensions of finitely generated K-algebras
proofSteps: The principal-ideal height bound alone does not supply the asserted global dimension inequality. The formerly cited ringKrullDim_le_ringKrullDim_quotient_add_spanFinrank also requires (z−ξ)A ≤ jacobson A, absent here (for A=K[z], jacobson A=0). A finite-type domain dimension formula/equidimensional hypersurface argument, with its precise localisation or catenary inputs, is still required; see the existing affine-family dimension gap. This proof outline is conditional until that input is supplied.

dim A ≥ dim A/(z − ξ) + 1: a chain of primes containing (z − ξ) starts at a prime 𝔓 over (z − ξ)K[z]; flat ⇒ going down (Ideal.height_eq_height_add_of_liesOver_of_hasGoingDown) gives a prime below 𝔓 lying over 0, lengthening the chain.

dim A = trdeg_K Frac(A): Noether normalization (exists_integral_inj_algHom_of_fg) makes A integral over a polynomial ring in trdeg variables, whose dimension is the number of variables (MvPolynomial.ringKrullDim_of_isNoetherianRing); integral extensions preserve dimension (going up and incomparability; see gaps).
trdeg_K Frac(A) = 1 + trdeg_{K(z)} Frac(A) since z is transcendental over K (tower formula trdeg_add_eq).
acceptance: A = K[z, X]: fibres K[X], of dimension 1 = 2 − 1.
A = K[z, X]/(zX − 1) has empty fibre at ξ = 0 (A/zA = 0), which the nonemptiness hypothesis excludes.

sources.match: The dimension comparison of the fibre at ξ with the generic fibre, used to pass from Beukers' lifting to transcendence degrees.

nodes.title: E-functions form a differential ring
nodes.statement: If a and b are E-functions then so are a + b, the Hurwitz product hurwitzMul a b (the product of the power series Σ a_n zⁿ/n! and Σ b_n zⁿ/n!) and the shift n ↦ a_{n+1} (the derivative).
hypotheses: Geometric normalisation of the arithmetic conditions
proofSteps: D-finiteness of sums, products and derivatives (d-finite-power-series API).
|σ(a_n + b_n)| ≤ 2C^{n+1}; den(a₀ + b₀, …) ≤ den(a)·den(b).
Product: the n-th coefficient Σ_k C(n, k) a_k b_{n−k} has conjugates ≤ 2ⁿC^{n+1}·C and denominators ≤ D^{2(n+1)}.
acceptance: exp · exp = e^{2z} (a_n = 2ⁿ) is an E-function.
The product of the E-functions eᶻ and (z − 1)eᶻ is (z − 1)e^{2z}.

nodes.title: Monomials in solutions of a first-order system solve a first-order system
nodes.statement: If F = (f₁, …, f_n) satisfies T(z)F′ = M(z)F with T ∈ ℂ[z] and M ∈ M_n(ℂ[z]), then for every N the vector of monomials f^e = ∏ f_i^{e_i}, |e| = N, satisfies T(z)(f^e)′ = Σ_{e′} M′_{e,e′} f^{e′} for a matrix M′ with polynomial entries (in the entries of M); in particular its singularities lie among the zeros of T. If the f_i are E-functions so are the f^e.
hypotheses: Polynomial (not rational) coefficients after clearing denominators
proofSteps: Leibniz rule: T·(f^e)′ = Σ_i e_i f^{e − δ_i}·T f_i′ = Σ_i e_i f^{e−δ_i} Σ_j M_{ij} f_j, and f^{e − δ_i}f_j is a monomial of degree N.
E-functions: e-functions-form-a-ring.
acceptance: For F = (eᶻ) (T = 1, M = (1)) the monomials e^{Nz} satisfy (e^{Nz})′ = N e^{Nz}.

sources.match: Verbatim step.

nodes.title: Division of a rational E-function by z − 1 at a zero
nodes.statement: If a is an E-function with rational coefficients and f(1) = 0 (f = eFun a), then g(z) = f(z)/(1 − z) is an E-function; its coefficients are b_n = n!·Σ_{k≤n} a_k/k!.
hypotheses: Rational coefficients (the general algebraic case needs beukers-vanishing-theorem)
proofSteps: g is entire since f(1) = 0; b_n/n! = Σ_{k≤n} a_k/k! = −Σ_{k>n} a_k/k!.
|a_k| ≤ B·C^k gives |b_n| ≤ B·n!·Σ_{k≥n} C^k/k! ≤ B·Cⁿ·e^C (k! ≥ n!(k − n)!).
den(b₀, …, b_n) ≤ den(a₀, …, a_n); g is D-finite (product of f and the rational function 1/(1 − z)).

sources.match: The step, with the estimates of the source.
The restriction to rational coefficients.

nodes.title: Shidlovskii's lemma (non-vanishing of the determinant of derived approximations)
nodes.statement: Let f be a vector of power series solving f′ = A(z)f, A ∈ M_n(ℂ(z)), with f₁, …, f_n linearly independent over ℂ(z). Let 0 < ε < 1 and N, M positive integers, and let Q, P₁, …, P_n be polynomials of degree ≤ N, not all zero, with Qf − P = O(z^{N+M}). Let Δ(z) be the determinant of the vectors (D − A)^m P, m = 0, …, n − 1. If M > N(1 − ε)/n and N is sufficiently large (in terms of A, f and ε) then Δ ≢ 0. (Lemma I: if Σ P_i f_i has vanishing order ≥ (n − ε)N, the determinant of (D + Aᵗ)^i P, i < n, is nonzero for N large.)
hypotheses: ℂ(z)-linear independence of the f_i
N large in terms of A, f and ε
proofSteps: Lemma I (AWS Theorem 6.2.6): the ℂ(z)-span of the derived vectors has a basis of bounded degree (Proposition 6.2.1, via differentially invariant subspaces, Lemmas 6.2.3–6.2.4 and exterior powers); if its dimension r were < n, some linear form in the f_i would vanish to order > (n − r − ε)N − r²t, contradicting Lemma 6.2.5 (bounded vanishing order of forms of bounded degree).
Lemma II (AWS Theorem 6.2.7, used in Chudnovsky's theorem): stated in the source with 'Proof. To be added'; see gaps.
acceptance: n = 1, f = eᶻ: Δ = P, nonzero whenever P ≠ 0.

sources.match: The statement; the source's proof of Lemma II is missing.

nodes.title: Chudnovsky's theorem: G-function systems satisfy Galochkin's condition
nodes.statement: Let (f₁, …, f_n) be a solution of y′ = G(z)y, G ∈ M_n(Q̄(z)), consisting of G-functions linearly independent over Q̄(z). Fix a nonzero polynomial T with T and M := TG having algebraic-integer coefficients. Write y^{(m)}/m! = B_m y and P_m := T^m B_m. The system satisfies Galochkin’s condition: the least positive integer q_s for which every coefficient of q_s P_m is an algebraic integer for 0 ≤ m ≤ s obeys q_s ≤ C^s for some C > 0 and every s ≥ 1. Equivalently use the unnormalised iterates A_m defined by y^{(m)} = A_m y and clear T^m A_m/m!; divide by the factorial exactly once.
hypotheses: The G-functions are Q̄(z)-linearly independent. A common number field for their coefficients and the system is a derived finite-coefficient-field comparison, not a new theorem hypothesis; that comparison remains part of the recorded DT.5 gap.
T ≠ 0 and T, TG have algebraic-integer coefficients after a common scaling, as assumed in AWS §5.2.
B_m is the divided derivative matrix. The additional /m! in the inherited denominator definition was erroneous; AWS §4.4 uses unnormalised A_m and §5.2 changes to divided B_m.
proofSteps: Choose by Siegel's lemma (Mathlib NumberField.house.exists_ne_zero_int_vec_house_le) polynomials Q, P of degree ≤ N with Qf − P = O(z^{N+M}) and small integral coefficients, M = N/(2n).
Differentiate: (T^m/m!)Q^{(m)}f − T^m P_m = O(z^{N+M−m}) with P_m = (D − G)^m P/m!, so T^m P_m has integral coefficients for m ≤ s = [N/(2n(t + 1))].

Use divided B_s throughout: AWS Lemma 5.2.1 gives B_s R(0) = Σ_{j=0}^s (−1)^j/(s−j)! D^{s−j}R(j), with R(j) formed from P_h=(D−G)^hP/h!. Shidlovskii’s lemma supplies invertibility of R(0). Bound an integral multiple of det R(0) and its conjugates to obtain an exponential integer denominator bound for T^m B_m. The detailed coefficient-divisibility, determinant-height and parameter-rounding lemmas are not yet decomposed; see the explicit gap.
acceptance: For y′ = y/(1−z), f = 1/(1−z), T=1−z and M=1: A_m=m!/(1−z)^m, B_m=(1−z)^{-m}, P_m=1 and q_s=1. Dividing B_m again by m! instead gives q_s=s!, which is not exponentially bounded.
For y′=y with T=M=1, P_m=1/m! and q_s=s!; the exponential solution is an E-function, not a G-function.

sources.locator: Theorem 4.4.3, p. 20, and proof in Section 5.2, pp. 21-22
sources.match: Theorem 4.4.3 with Definition 4.4.1. The §4.4 matrices are unnormalised; the §5.2 lemma explicitly normalises them by 1/s!. The packet now uses B_s for the latter and omits a second factorial. Detailed proof closure remains partial.
The first recursion uses unnormalised iterates. Lemma 5.2.1 on p.22 switches to y^{(s)}/s!=G_s y; the two conventions must not be combined.

nodes.title: The minimal equation of a G-function is regular singular at 0
nodes.statement: Let g be a nonzero G-function and L its minimal differential equation of order n. Then z = 0 is a regular point or a regular singular point of L: writing a minimal equation Σ p_i g^{(i)} = 0, ord₀(p_n) − ord₀(p_i) ≤ n − i for all i with p_i ≠ 0 (Fuchs' criterion).
hypotheses: g a G-function; L of minimal order
proofSteps: The first-order system of L satisfies Galochkin's condition by chudnovsky-galochkin-condition.

Proposition 5.3.1: write zⁿy^{(n)} = Σ B_k z^k y^{(k)}; if λ := max_k v(B_{n−k})/k > 0, the limits α_{m,r} = lim z^{(m−r)λ}A_{m,r} exist, are nonzero infinitely often and are powers of a companion matrix, so the denominators of the coefficients of z^m y^{(m)}/m! grow faster than exponentially, contradicting Galochkin's condition.
acceptance: −log(1 − z): minimal equation (1 − z)y″ − y′ = 0, regular at 0.
exp is not a G-function; its equation y′ = y is regular at 0 anyway (the statement is not an equivalence).

sources.match: The statement, proved in the source from Theorem 4.4.3 and Proposition 5.3.1.

nodes.title: The Laplace transform of an E-function is a G-function at 1/x
nodes.statement: Let a be an E-function, f=eFun a, and g=Σaₙzⁿ a G-function. For sufficiently large real x, ∫₀∞exp(−xt)f(t)dt=x⁻¹g(x⁻¹). For u(t)=t^mf(t), the derivative identity is ∫₀∞exp(−xt)u^{(k)}(t)dt=x^k(−d/dx)^m[x⁻¹g(x⁻¹)]−Σ_{j=0}^{k−1}x^{k−1−j}u^{(j)}(0). The boundary polynomial must be retained. The operator transfer used by André requires a formal Laurent-series transform or a separate argument cancelling the boundary polynomial, recorded as a gap.
hypotheses: x real and larger than the geometric growth constant of the a_n
proofSteps: |a_n| ≤ Cⁿ⁺¹ gives |f(t)| ≤ C e^{Ct}, so the integral converges for x > C.
Term-by-term: ∫_0^∞ e^{−xt}tⁿ/n! dt = x^{−n−1} (dominated convergence).
Repeated integration by parts gives the displayed finite boundary sum; it cannot be dropped for arbitrary k,m. The source equality omits it (E20).
acceptance: f=eᶻ,k=1,m=0: Laplace(f′)=1/(x−1), while xLaplace(f)=x/(x−1); their difference is f(0)=1.

nodes.title: André's theorem: E-functions satisfy equations singular only at 0 and ∞
nodes.statement: Every E-function f satisfies a differential equation z^m y^{(m)} + Σ_{k=0}^{m−1} z^k q_k(z) y^{(k)} = 0 with q_k ∈ Q̄[z] of degree ≤ m − k. In particular f satisfies a nonzero linear differential equation whose only singularities are 0 and ∞.
hypotheses: The equation need not be the minimal one; the minimal equation may have (apparent) singularities elsewhere
proofSteps: g = Σ a_n zⁿ is a G-function (isGFunction_iff_isEFunction); its minimal equation is regular singular at 0 (g-operator-regular-singularity-at-zero), so (1/x)g(1/x) satisfies Σ A_{k,m}x^k(−d/dx)^m u = 0 with A_{K,M} ≠ 0 and A_{K,m} = 0 for m < M, K the largest x-degree (regularity at x = ∞ ↔ regularity of g at 0).

The source transfers the operator using a Laplace derivative identity with omitted boundary terms. The corrected integral identity is DT.5/laplace-transform-of-e-function; a formal transform/cancellation argument and preservation of the claimed leading coefficient remain gapped. The André theorem statement is retained without a closed proof claim.
acceptance: f = (z − 1)eᶻ: the equation y″ − 2y′ + y = 0 has no singularity at 1, while the minimal equation (z − 1)y′ = zy does.
f = eᶻ: m = 1, zy′ − zy = 0 (q₀ = −z of degree 1 ≤ 1).

nodes.title: The minimal equation of an E-function has holomorphic solutions away from 0
nodes.statement: Let f be an E-function and L its minimal differential equation. At every point z₀ ≠ 0 the equation Ly = 0 has a basis of solutions holomorphic at z₀; hence every singularity of L other than 0 is apparent.
hypotheses: Uses the local solution space of a linear differential equation (holomorphic-solutions-of-linear-systems)
proofSteps: andre-theorem-on-e-operators gives an operator L′ singular only at 0, ∞ with L′f = 0; since L is minimal, L′ = M∘L for an operator M (right division in Q̄(z)[∂]).
Solutions of L near z₀ ≠ 0 are solutions of L′, and z₀ is a regular point of L′, so they are holomorphic at z₀ (holomorphic-solutions-of-linear-systems); L has order-many independent such solutions.
acceptance: f = (z − 1)eᶻ: the solutions of (z − 1)y′ = zy are c(z − 1)eᶻ, holomorphic at 1.

nodes.title: André: a rational E-function vanishing at 1 forces an apparent singularity
nodes.statement: Let f be an E-function with rational coefficients, L its minimal equation, and suppose f(1) = 0. Then every solution of Ly = 0 near z = 1 vanishes at 1; in particular z = 1 is an apparent singularity of L.
hypotheses: Rational coefficients
Solutions of L near 1 (holomorphic-solutions-of-linear-systems)

Use a nonzero f and a positive-order minimal equation when claiming an apparent singularity. For f=0, a minimal order-zero equation has no such singularity; the all-solutions-vanish clause alone is vacuous.
proofSteps: g = f/(1 − z) is an E-function (rational-e-function-divided-by-vanishing-factor), with minimal operator L∘(z − 1).
andre-holomorphic-solution-basis for g: the kernel of L∘(z − 1) near 1 is spanned by holomorphic functions, so the kernel of L consists of (z − 1)·holomorphic functions.
acceptance: f = (z − 1)eᶻ vanishes at 1 and its minimal equation (z − 1)y′ = zy is singular (apparently) at 1.

Transcendence of π (AWS Corollary 3.4.3): if 2πi were algebraic, the product of the conjugates of e^{2πiz} − 1 would contradict this corollary, as exponential polynomials satisfy constant-coefficient equations.

nodes.title: Beukers: at a nonzero algebraic zero of an E-function all solutions of its minimal equation vanish
nodes.statement: Let f be an E-function with minimal equation L of order n, and ξ ∈ Q̄^× with f(ξ) = 0. Then all solutions of Ly = 0 vanish at z = ξ; in particular ξ is an apparent singularity of L.
hypotheses: ξ ≠ 0 algebraic
Needs differential Galois groups (gap) and local solutions (holomorphic-solutions-of-linear-systems)

Use a nonzero f and a positive-order minimal equation when claiming an apparent singularity. For f=0, a minimal order-zero equation has no such singularity; the all-solutions-vanish clause alone is vacuous.
proofSteps: Reduce to ξ = 1 (replace f(z) by f(ξz)). Let f^{σ_1}, …, f^{σ_r} be the Galois conjugates (IsEFunction.map_ringEquiv) and F = ∏ f^{σ_i}, an E-function with rational coefficients vanishing at 1; by andre-vanishing-corollary all solutions of F's minimal equation vanish at 1.

Lemma 2.3: the images of f under the identity component G° of its differential Galois group span the full solution space of L (else a lower-order equation over the fixed field, summed over G/G°, contradicts minimality).
Lemma 2.4: for an algebraic subgroup H ⊆ G₁ × ⋯ × G_r projecting onto each factor, H° projects onto each G_i°.

H° = ∪_i H_i with H_i = {h : π_i(h)v_i vanishes at 1} Zariski closed; H° connected gives H_i = H° for some i, so G_i° maps f^{σ_i} into the solutions vanishing at 1, whose span is everything by Lemma 2.3; conjugate back to f.
acceptance: f = (z − 2)eᶻ, ξ = 2: minimal equation (z − 2)y′ = (z − 1)y, all solutions c(z − 2)eᶻ vanish at 2.

sources.locator: Lemma 2.3, Lemma 2.4 and Theorem 2.5 with proof, pp. 4-6

nodes.title: A basis of polynomial relations with full-rank specialisations
nodes.statement: Let f₁, …, f_n be power series whose K(z)-span has dimension m (K an algebraically closed subfield of ℂ, as in the source K=Q̄ or the prototype K=ℂ). There is a K[z]-basis C₁, …, C_{n−m} of the module of polynomial relations {c ∈ K[z]ⁿ : Σ c_i f_i = 0} such that for every ξ the specialised vectors C_j(ξ) are linearly independent, i.e. the (n − m) × n matrix (C_{ji}(ξ)) has rank n − m.
hypotheses: K is algebraically closed for the stated linear-factor descent proof. The suggested theorem is over ℂ; the source is over Q̄. A general subfield version needs an irreducible-factor/PID saturation argument.
proofSteps: Start from any n − m independent relations; let D be the gcd of the maximal minors.
If D(ξ) = 0, a K-combination of rows vanishes at ξ; divide that row by z − ξ (still a relation because the module of relations is saturated: ℂ[[z]] is a domain) and replace it, lowering deg D.
When D is constant the rows form a K[z]-basis of all relations and specialise to full rank everywhere.
acceptance: f = (1, 1): relations c₁ + c₂ = 0, basis (1, −1), full rank at every ξ.
The relation (z, −z) for f = (1, 1) specialises to 0 at ξ = 0; the lemma replaces it by (1, −1).

sources.match: The statement (matrix elided) and the gcd-of-minors argument.

nodes.title: Beukers: linear relations between values come from functional relations
nodes.statement: Let f₁, …, f_n be E-functions solving T(z)f′ = M(z)f with T ∈ Q̄[z], M ∈ M_n(Q̄[z]) (T the common denominator of A = M/T), and ξ ∈ Q̄ with ξT(ξ) ≠ 0. Every Q̄-linear relation Σ λ_i f_i(ξ) = 0 is the specialisation at ξ of a Q̄[z]-linear relation Σ c_i(z) f_i(z) = 0 with c_i(ξ) = λ_i. In particular (Corollary 1.4), if f₁, …, f_n are Q̄(z)-linearly independent then f₁(ξ), …, f_n(ξ) are Q̄-linearly independent.
hypotheses: ξ ≠ 0 and T(ξ) ≠ 0 (at zeros of T the system itself produces relations M(ξ)f(ξ) = 0)
proofSteps: Suppose a relation λ does not come from specialisation; choose relation-module-basis-with-full-rank-specialisations and polynomials A_i with A_i(ξ) = λ_i and chosen derivatives at ξ so that F = Σ A_i f_i has minimal equation of order m (the Q̄(z)-rank) with ξ a regular point (the determinant det M_m does not vanish at ξ).
F is an E-function (e-functions-form-a-ring) with F(ξ) = Σλ_i f_i(ξ) = 0, so by beukers-vanishing-theorem ξ is a singularity of its minimal equation: contradiction.
acceptance: Lindemann–Weierstrass (lindemann-weierstrass-via-e-functions) is the case f_i = e^{β_i z}, T = 1, ξ = 1.
At ξ = 1 with f = ((z − 1)eᶻ, eᶻ) and T = z − 1 the hypothesis fails and indeed f₁(1) = 0.

sources.match: Verbatim; Corollary 1.4 is the linear-independence form.

nodes.title: Beukers' refined Siegel–Shidlovskii theorem
nodes.statement: Let f₁, …, f_n be E-functions solving T(z)f′ = M(z)f with T ∈ Q̄[z], M ∈ M_n(Q̄[z]) (T the common denominator of A = M/T), and ξ ∈ Q̄ with ξT(ξ) ≠ 0. For every homogeneous polynomial P ∈ Q̄[X₁, …, X_n] with P(f₁(ξ), …, f_n(ξ)) = 0 there is Q ∈ Q̄[z][X₁, …, X_n], homogeneous in the X_i of the same degree, with Q(z, f₁(z), …, f_n(z)) ≡ 0 and Q(ξ, X) = P(X). (Adding f₀ = 1 removes the word 'homogeneous'.)
hypotheses: As in beukers-linear-relations-theorem
proofSteps: Apply beukers-linear-relations-theorem to the vector of monomials of degree deg P (monomials-of-e-functions-solve-a-system: same singular set T = 0); the relation P becomes a linear relation between the values of the monomials.
acceptance: With f = (1, eᶻ) and ξ = 1: e is transcendental (no functional polynomial relation between 1 and eᶻ).
With f = (1, J₀(z), J₀′(z)) the algebraic independence of J₀, J₀′ over Q̄(z) (Siegel) gives the algebraic independence of J₀(ξ), J₀′(ξ) for algebraic ξ ≠ 0.

sources.match: Theorem 1.2's conclusion, which Theorem 1.3 asserts for every ξ with ξT(ξ) ≠ 0.

nodes.title: The Siegel–Shidlovskii theorem
nodes.statement: Let f₁, …, f_n be E-functions solving T(z)f′ = M(z)f with T ∈ Q̄[z], M ∈ M_n(Q̄[z]) (T the common denominator of A = M/T), and ξ ∈ Q̄ with ξT(ξ) ≠ 0. Then trdeg_Q̄ Q̄(f₁(ξ), …, f_n(ξ)) = trdeg_{Q̄(z)} Q̄(z)(f₁(z), …, f_n(z)) (equivalently over ℂ(z), by transcendence-over-algebraic-rational-functions).
hypotheses: ξT(ξ) ≠ 0
proofSteps: Let I ⊂ Q̄[z][X] be the (prime) ideal of polynomial relations and J ⊂ Q̄[X] the ideal of relations between the values. beukers-refined-siegel-shidlovskii (inhomogeneous form) gives J = {Q(ξ, X) : Q ∈ I}.

Q̄[z][X]/I is a domain, torsion-free over Q̄[z] (z − ξ is not a zero divisor modulo I), so its fibre Q̄[X]/J at ξ has Krull dimension equal to the transcendence degree of its generic fibre (fibre-dimension-over-the-affine-line).
J is the ideal of the point (f(ξ)), so dim Q̄[X]/J = trdeg of the values.
acceptance: f = (e^{β_1 z}, …, e^{β_n z}) with β_i ℚ-linearly independent algebraic: the functions are algebraically independent, so e^{β_i} are algebraically independent (Lindemann–Weierstrass, Evertse Corollary 4.10, DT.3).
The classical proof (Siegel's method with Shidlovskii's lemma) is an alternative route; André (2014) gives a third via generalised differential Galois theory.

sources.match: Verbatim (the system elided).

The source assumes relative algebraic closure and a transcendence-degree equality, and then deduces lifting. It is a comparison source, not an independent proof of the packet’s dimension equality from torsion-freeness alone.

nodes.title: Division of an E-function by z − ξ at an algebraic zero
nodes.statement: If f is an E-function and ξ ∈ Q̄^× with f(ξ) = 0, then f(z)/(z − ξ) is an E-function.
hypotheses: ξ ≠ 0 algebraic
proofSteps: Reduce to ξ = 1. By beukers-vanishing-theorem all solutions of the minimal equation vanish at 1, hence (conjugating the equation) every Galois conjugate f^σ vanishes at 1.
The estimate of rational-e-function-divided-by-vanishing-factor applies to each of the finitely many conjugates, giving the geometric bound on all conjugates of the new coefficients.
acceptance: f = (z − ξ)e^{z}: the quotient is eᶻ.

sources.match: Verbatim.

nodes.title: Beukers: E-function systems reduce to systems singular only at 0
nodes.statement: Let f₁, …, f_n be Q̄(z)-linearly independent E-functions solving a first-order system over Q̄(z). There are E-functions e₁, …, e_n and a matrix B ∈ M_n(Q̄[z]) with det B ≠ 0 such that f = B·e and e solves a system with coefficients in Q̄[z, 1/z].
hypotheses: Q̄(z)-linear independence
proofSteps: Take a fundamental matrix F of the system whose first column is f (images of f under the differential Galois group; holomorphic away from 0 by andre-holomorphic-solution-basis); W = det F satisfies W′ = tr(A)W, so its zeros α are singularities, hence algebraic.

At such α a relation M(α)f(α) = 0 gives, after a constant change of basis, a component vanishing at α; beukers-vanishing-theorem makes the whole first row of MF vanish at α, and e-function-division-by-vanishing-factor divides by z − α keeping E-functions.
Each step lowers the vanishing order of det F at α; iterate over all zeros of W.
acceptance: f = ((z − 1)eᶻ): B = (z − 1), e = eᶻ solving e′ = e.

sources.locator: Theorem 1.5, p. 3, and proof in Section 4, pp. 8-9
sources.match: The conclusion of Theorem 1.5.

nodes.title: Lindemann–Weierstrass as a case of Beukers' theorem
nodes.statement: For pairwise distinct algebraic β₁, …, β_n, the numbers e^{β₁}, …, e^{β_n} are linearly independent over Q̄.
hypotheses: β_i distinct and algebraic
proofSteps: f_i = e^{β_i z} are E-functions (e-function test: a_n = β_iⁿ has geometric size and denominators), linearly independent over Q̄(z) and solving f′ = diag(β)f with T = 1.
beukers-linear-relations-theorem at ξ = 1.
acceptance: This is Evertse's Theorem 4.8 (Baker's form), node DT.3 lindemann-weierstrass-in-bakers-form: the two proofs must agree on the statement.
With β=(0,1), ℚ̄-linear independence of1 ande already says that e is transcendental.

sources.match: The derivation.

nodes.title: Linear independence of values of G-functions at rationals close to 0
nodes.statement: Let f₁, …, f_n be G-functions with rational coefficients solving y′ = Gy over Q̄(z) and linearly independent over Q̄(z). There is C > 0 such that f₁(a/b), …, f_n(a/b) are linearly independent over ℚ for all integers a ≠ 0, b > 0 with b > C|a|^{n+1}.
hypotheses: Rational coefficients; the point a/b must be very close to 0 relative to its height
proofSteps: chudnovsky-galochkin-condition shows the system satisfies Galochkin's condition.

Galochkin's theorem (Siegel's method for G-functions: Siegel's lemma, Padé-type approximations, Shidlovskii's lemma) gives the linear independence; the public source only sketches it (AWS §6.3, 'To be finished'), see gaps.
acceptance: For f=(1,−log(1−z)), n=2, the displayed condition is b>C|a|³. The conclusion gives irrationality of log(1−a/b); a² would be the wrong exponent for this two-component tuple.

sources.match: The conclusion of Galochkin's theorem; with Theorem 4.4.3 the Galochkin condition is automatic.

nodes.title: Algebraic independence over ℂ(z) of series with algebraic coefficients
nodes.statement: Let f₁, …, f_n ∈ ℂ[[z]] have algebraic coefficients. Then f₁, …, f_n are algebraically independent over ℂ(z) iff no nonzero polynomial P ∈ Q̄[z][X₁, …, X_n] satisfies P(z, f₁, …, f_n) = 0. Hence transcendence degrees over ℂ(z) and over Q̄(z) coincide for such series.
hypotheses: Algebraic coefficients
proofSteps: Given a relation with coefficients c_β ∈ ℂ[z], write all complex coefficients in a Q̄-basis e₁, …, e_s of their Q̄-span: c_β = Σ_k e_k c_{β,k} with c_{β,k} ∈ Q̄[z].

Then Σ_k e_k (Σ_β c_{β,k} f^β) = 0 in ℂ[[z]] with inner sums in Q̄[[z]]; comparing coefficients and using Q̄-independence of the e_k, every inner sum vanishes, and one of them is a nonzero Q̄[z]-relation.
acceptance: f = (eᶻ): no Q̄[z]-relation, hence none over ℂ(z).
Fails without algebraic coefficients: f = (πz) is algebraic over ℂ(z) but, over Q̄(z), transcendental.

sources.match: The source states Siegel–Shidlovskii over ℂ(z) whereas Beukers states it over Q̄(z); this lemma reconciles them.

nodes.title: Nishioka's theorem (Mahler's method)
nodes.statement: Let q ≥ 2 and f₁, …, f_n power series with algebraic coefficients, convergent on |z| < ρ, solving the Mahler system f(z) = A(z)f(z^q) with A ∈ GL_n(Q̄(z)), and let α ∈ Q̄ with 0 < |α| < ρ be a regular point. Then trdeg_Q̄ Q̄(f₁(α), …, f_n(α)) = trdeg_{Q̄(z)} Q̄(z)(f₁(z), …, f_n(z)).
hypotheses: α regular (mahler-regular-point); 0 < |α| < ρ
The Mahler analogue of the Siegel–Shidlovskii theorem
proofSteps: Mahler's method: construct an auxiliary polynomial E(z) = P(z, f(z)) vanishing to high order at 0 (Siegel's lemma), iterate the functional equation to evaluate at α^{q^k} → 0, and compare the analytic upper bound with Liouville-type lower bounds; Nishioka's algebraic independence criterion upgrades transcendence to the transcendence-degree equality.
The complete proof is in Nishioka's monograph (LNM 1631), which is not public; see gaps.
acceptance: For the Fredholm series (n = 2 with 1): trdeg Q̄(f(α)) = 1, i.e. Σ α^{2^k} is transcendental.
Compatible with mahler-homogeneous-relations-lift, which refines it.

sources.match: The hypotheses; the conclusion is the transcendence-degree equality.

nodes.title: Philippon, Adamczewski–Faverjon: homogeneous relations between Mahler values lift
nodes.statement: Let q ≥ 2 and f₁, …, f_n power series with algebraic coefficients, convergent on the open unit disc, solving the Mahler system f(z) = A(z)f(z^q) with A ∈ GL_n(Q̄(z)), and let α ∈ Q̄ with 0 < |α| < 1 be a regular point. For every homogeneous P ∈ Q̄[X] with P(f(α)) = 0 there is Q ∈ Q̄[z][X], homogeneous of the same degree in X, with Q(z, f(z)) = 0 and Q(α, X) = P(X).
hypotheses: α regular; homogeneous relations (inhomogeneous ones follow by adding f₀ = 1 with A replaced by diag(A, 1))
proofSteps: Adamczewski–Faverjon §3: from nishioka-theorem, by the argument of Nesterenko–Shidlovskii and Beukers adapted to Mahler systems (induction on the dimension of the Zariski closure of the orbit, using that the system maps the ideal of relations at α^{q^k} to that at α^{q^{k+1}}); decomposition into nodes is recorded as remaining.
acceptance: For (1, f) with f the Fredholm series: the only homogeneous relations at α are specialisations, so 1 and f(α) are linearly independent.

sources.match: The conclusion of Theorem 1.4 (Theorem 1.2 is Philippon's inhomogeneous version).

nodes.title: Linear relations between Mahler values at regular points lift
nodes.statement: Let q ≥ 2 and f₁, …, f_n power series with algebraic coefficients, convergent on the open unit disc, solving the Mahler system f(z) = A(z)f(z^q) with A ∈ GL_n(Q̄(z)), and let α ∈ Q̄ with 0 < |α| < 1 be a regular point. Then Rel_Q̄(f₁(α), …, f_n(α)) = ev_α(Rel_{Q̄(z)}(f₁(z), …, f_n(z))); in particular, if f₁, …, f_n are Q̄(z)-linearly independent, f₁(α), …, f_n(α) are Q̄-linearly independent.
hypotheses: α regular
proofSteps: The degree-one case of mahler-homogeneous-relations-lift.
acceptance: Remark 1.6 of the source: linear independence of 1, f₁(α), …, f_n(α) needs 1, f₁, …, f_n independent over Q̄(z), which fails for automatic systems where Σ f_i = 1/(1 − z).

sources.match: The linear-independence form; the displayed equality Rel = ev_α(Rel) precedes it.

nodes.title: A Mahler value is transcendental or lies in the field of the data
nodes.statement: Let f be a q-Mahler function, α ∈ Q̄ with 0 < |α| < 1 not a pole of f, and k a number field containing α and the coefficients of f. Then f(α) is transcendental or f(α) ∈ k. More generally (Theorem 1.7), if f₁(α), …, f_n(α) are linearly dependent over Q̄ they are linearly dependent over k.
hypotheses: No regularity assumption on α (only that α is not a pole)
In Lean the series is assumed to converge at α, which is stronger than 'not a pole'
proofSteps: Adamczewski–Faverjon §§4–5: iterate the system to reach a regular point α^{q^ℓ} (Theorem 1.10), apply mahler-linear-relations-lift there and descend the relations with the matrix A_ℓ(z) = A(z)A(z^q)⋯A(z^{q^{ℓ−1}}) (Theorem 1.9); Galois-descent of linear relations from Q̄ to k; decomposition into nodes is recorded as remaining.
acceptance: The alternative cannot be removed: AF §7 give transcendental Mahler functions taking algebraic values at algebraic points.
For automatic series and rational α this is Cobham's conjecture (1968).

sources.match: Verbatim.

nodes.title: The lacunary series Σ z^{2^n} is not a rational function
nodes.statement: There are no polynomials p, r with r ≠ 0 and r(z)·Σ_{n≥0} z^{2^n} = p(z) in ℂ[[z]].
proofSteps: If r·f = p with deg r = d, the coefficients c_m of f satisfy Σ_{i≤d} r_i c_{m−i} = 0 for m > deg p, a linear recurrence of order ≤ d with r_0 or some r_i ≠ 0.

Normalise so that the recurrence expresses c_m through c_{m−1}, …, c_{m−d} (divide by the lowest nonzero r_i); for 2^k > 2d + deg p the d coefficients before 2^k are 0 and c_{2^k} = 1, a contradiction.
acceptance: Equivalently 1 and f are Q̄(z)-linearly independent, the input of mahler-fredholm-transcendence.

sources.match: Context (transcendental Mahler functions are far from rational); the lemma is proved by the elementary gap argument.

nodes.title: Mahler's theorem: Σ α^{2^n} is transcendental
nodes.statement: For every algebraic α with 0 < |α| < 1, the number Σ_{n≥0} α^{2^n} is transcendental.
hypotheses: α algebraic, 0 < |α| < 1
proofSteps: F = (1, f) with f = Σ z^{2^n} solves F(z) = A(z)F(z²), A = [[1, 0], [z, 1]] (f(z) = z + f(z²)); every 0 < |α| < 1 is regular (mahler-regular-point test).
1, f are Q̄(z)-linearly independent (lacunary-series-not-rational), so by mahler-linear-relations-lift 1 and f(α) are Q̄-linearly independent: f(α) ∉ Q̄.
acceptance: α = 1/2: Σ 2^{−2^n} is transcendental (Kempner's number).

sources.match: Mahler's original application, derived here from Corollary 1.5.

nodes.title: Nesterenko's theorem
nodes.statement: For every τ in the upper half-plane, with q = e^{2πiτ} (so 0 < |q| < 1), at least three of the four numbers q, P(q) = E₂(τ), Q(q) = E₄(τ), R(q) = E₆(τ) are algebraically independent over ℚ. Here E₂, E₄, E₆ are Mathlib's EisensteinSeries.E2, ModularForm.E₄, ModularForm.E₆ (normalised with constant term 1, P = 1 − 24Σσ₁(n)qⁿ, Q = 1 + 240Σσ₃(n)qⁿ, R = 1 − 504Σσ₅(n)qⁿ).
hypotheses: Every q with 0 < |q| < 1 is e^{2πiτ} for some τ ∈ ℍ
proofSteps: Nesterenko (1996): a multiplicity (zero) estimate for polynomials in z, P(z), Q(z), R(z) via the Ramanujan differential system, an auxiliary polynomial constructed by Siegel's lemma, and Philippon's criterion for algebraic independence; the Barré-Sirieix–Diaz–Gramain–Philibert theorem (q or J(q) transcendental) enters the arithmetic estimates.
No public complete source was obtained; see gaps.
acceptance: q = e^{−2π} (τ = i): with E₂(i) = 3/π and E₆(i) = 0 it gives the algebraic independence of π, e^π and E₄(i) (hence of π, e^π, Γ(1/4) via Chowla–Selberg).
The analogous statement with only q and J(q) is the Barré-Sirieix–Diaz–Gramain–Philibert theorem.

sources.locator: Section 4, Theorem 17 and the statement preceding it, p. 443
sources.match: Verbatim (quoting Nesterenko's theorem as stated in Kontsevich–Zagier §2.4).

nodes.title: E₂(i) = 3/π and E₆(i) = 0
nodes.statement: At τ = i: E₂(i) = 3/π, E₆(i) = 0, and q(i) = e^{−2π}.
proofSteps: E₂ transformation under S (Mathlib EisensteinSeries.E2_slash_action with D2_S): E₂(−1/τ) = τ²E₂(τ) + 6τ/(πi); at τ = i, −1/i = i gives E₂(i) = −E₂(i) + 6/π.
E₆ is a weight-6 modular form: E₆(−1/τ) = τ⁶E₆(τ); at τ = i, E₆(i) = −E₆(i).
acceptance: Numerically E₂(i) ≈ 0.9549 = 3/π.

sources.match: The special values used.

nodes.title: π and e^π are algebraically independent
nodes.statement: π and e^π are algebraically independent over ℚ.
proofSteps: nesterenko-theorem at τ = i: three of e^{−2π}, E₂(i), E₄(i), E₆(i) are algebraically independent; E₆(i) = 0 (eisenstein-series-values-at-i), so the three are e^{−2π}, 3/π, E₄(i).
Algebraic independence of e^{−2π}, 3/π, E₄(i) implies that of e^{2π}, π, hence of e^π, π (e^{2π} = (e^π)²).
acceptance: Consistent with Schanuel's conjecture, which predicts e and π independent (not implied).

sources.match: The corollary (without Γ(1/4), which needs the Chowla–Selberg formula).

nodes.title: Ax: a minimal F-linear dependence among the forms dy/y − dx has constant coefficients
nodes.statement: Let F be a field of characteristic 0 with derivations D₁, …, D_k, C = ∩ ker D_j its constants, and x, y ∈ F^n with y_i ≠ 0 and D_j x_i = D_j y_i / y_i for all i, j; put ω_i := dy_i/y_i − dx_i ∈ Ω_{F/C}. If ω₁, …, ω_n are F-linearly dependent in Ω_{F/C}, then they are C-linearly dependent.
hypotheses: The exponential differential equation holds for every D_j
proofSteps: Take a minimal dependence Σ α_i ω_i = 0 with some α_{i₀} = 1.
Apply the Lie derivative L_D = D*∘d + d∘D* (D ∈ Δ): L_D(αω) = (Dα)ω + αL_Dω, D*ω_i = 0 by the differential equation and dω_i = 0 (closed forms), so Σ (Dα_i)ω_i = 0.
Minimality with Dα_{i₀} = 0 forces Dα_i = 0 for all i, i.e. α_i ∈ C.
acceptance: F = ℂ((t)), D = d/dt, x = (t, 2t), y = (eᵗ, e^{2t}) (formally): ω₂ = 2ω₁, a relation with constant coefficient 2.

sources.match: Step 1 of the proof (for semiabelian S; here S = G_m^n).

nodes.title: Ax: a constant relation among dy/y − dx forces an integer relation among the x_i modulo constants
nodes.statement: Let F be a field of characteristic 0 with derivations D₁, …, D_k, C = ∩ ker D_j its constants, and x, y ∈ F^n with y_i ≠ 0 and D_j x_i = D_j y_i / y_i for all i, j; put ω_i := dy_i/y_i − dx_i ∈ Ω_{F/C}. If Σ c_i ω_i = 0 with c ∈ Cⁿ nonzero, then there is a nonzero z ∈ ℤⁿ with Σ z_i x_i ∈ C.
hypotheses: Needs the structure of algebraic subgroups of G_aⁿ × G_mⁿ and Chevalley's indecomposability theorem (gap)

The cited orbit proof assumes algebraically closed constants C (Kirby Step2). Extending the theorem from arbitrary constant fields requires an algebraic extension and descent argument; it is recorded as a gap rather than silently imported.
proofSteps: η=Σcᵢ(dYᵢ/Yᵢ−dXᵢ) defines a group homomorphism on F-points to Ω(F/C); its kernel is a proper subgroup, not asserted to be an algebraic subgroup. Kirby’s Step2 constructs a separate algebraic subgroup inside this kernel from the orbit of a translated generic point.

Translating the C-locus of (x, y) to the identity and using Chevalley's indecomposability theorem, the group G generated by the orbit is a proper algebraic subgroup of ker η; by Kirby Lemma 3.6 it is J × H with H a proper algebraic subgroup of G_mⁿ (Step 3).
A proper algebraic subgroup of G_mⁿ lies in the kernel of a nontrivial character y ↦ ∏y_i^{z_i}; the exponential differential equation transfers this to Σ z_i x_i ∈ C (Step 4).
acceptance: x = (t, 2t): z = (2, −1) gives 2x₁ − x₂ = 0 ∈ C.

sources.locator: Section 3.3, Lemma 3.6 and Proposition 3.7 Steps 2-4, pp. 35-37
sources.match: The algebraic-group input of Steps 2–4.

nodes.title: Ax's theorem (Ax–Schanuel for the exponential)
nodes.statement: Let F be a field of characteristic 0 with derivations D₁, …, D_k, C = ∩ ker D_j its constants, and x, y ∈ F^n with y_i ≠ 0 and D_j x_i = D_j y_i / y_i for all i, j; put ω_i := dy_i/y_i − dx_i ∈ Ω_{F/C}. If x₁, …, x_n are ℚ-linearly independent modulo C, then trdeg_C C(x, y) ≥ n + rank(D_j x_i)_{j,i}. For one derivation with some D x_i ≠ 0: trdeg_C C(x, y) ≥ n + 1.
hypotheses: C is exactly the field of common constants
ℚ-linear independence modulo C (no Σ q_i x_i ∈ C)
proofSteps: Let E = C(x, y). dim_E Ω_{E/C} = trdeg_C E (kaehler-differentials-and-transcendence-degree).
The map D* : Ω_{E/C} ⊗ F → Fᵏ, ω ↦ (ω(D_j)), has rank rk(D_j x_i, D_j y_i) = rk(D_j x_i); its kernel has dimension trdeg − rank.

All ω_i lie in that kernel; if trdeg − rank < n they are F-linearly dependent, hence C-linearly dependent (ax-constant-coefficient-lemma), hence Σ z_i x_i ∈ C for a nonzero integer vector (ax-integer-relation-lemma), contradicting the hypothesis.
acceptance: F = ℂ((t)), x = (t), y = (eᵗ): trdeg ℂ(t, eᵗ) = 2 = 1 + 1.
Without independence: x = (t, 2t), y = (eᵗ, e^{2t}) has trdeg 2 < 2 + 1.

sources.match: The one-derivation statement.
The several-derivation form with the Jacobian rank, whose proof is followed.

nodes.title: Ax–Schanuel for formal power series
nodes.statement: Let f₁, …, f_n ∈ ℂ[[t₁, …, t_m]] be ℚ-linearly independent modulo ℂ. Then trdeg_ℂ ℂ(f₁, …, f_n, e^{f₁}, …, e^{f_n}) ≥ n + rk J(f), where J(f) = (∂f_i/∂t_j). In one variable, for f_i with zero constant term (n ≥ 1): trdeg ≥ n + 1.
hypotheses: e^{f} is defined for f with zero constant term by substitution into the exponential series (a constant term c multiplies e^f by e^c, which does not change transcendence degree over ℂ)
proofSteps: Apply ax-schanuel-theorem to the fraction field of ℂ[[t]] with the derivations ∂/∂t_j (common constants ℂ), x_i = f_i, y_i = e^{f_i} (∂_j e^{f} = e^{f}∂_j f).
acceptance: f = (t): trdeg ℂ(t, eᵗ) = 2.
f = (t, t²): trdeg ℂ(t, t², eᵗ, e^{t²}) = 3 = 2 + 1.

sources.match: Verbatim.

nodes.title: Weak Ax–Schanuel
nodes.statement: In the setting of ax-schanuel-power-series: trdeg_ℂ ℂ(f) + trdeg_ℂ ℂ(e^f) ≥ n + rk J(f).
proofSteps: trdeg ℂ(f, e^f) ≤ trdeg ℂ(f) + trdeg ℂ(e^f) (subadditivity), then ax-schanuel-power-series.

sources.match: Verbatim.

nodes.title: Ax–Lindemann–Weierstrass for the exponential
nodes.statement: In the setting of ax-schanuel-power-series, if moreover trdeg_ℂ ℂ(f) = rk J(f) (the germ f parametrises an algebraic variety), then e^{f₁}, …, e^{f_n} are algebraically independent over ℂ. Geometrically (with π : ℂⁿ → (ℂ^×)ⁿ the exponential): for an algebraic V ⊆ ℂⁿ, the Zariski closure of π(V) is a finite union of cosets of subtori; a maximal irreducible algebraic subvariety of π⁻¹(W), W ⊆ (ℂ^×)ⁿ algebraic, is a translate of a rational linear subspace.
hypotheses: ℚ-linear independence modulo ℂ
proofSteps: weak-ax-schanuel with trdeg ℂ(f) = rk J gives trdeg ℂ(e^f) ≥ n.

The geometric forms are Bakker–Tsimerman Corollaries 1.2.13–1.2.15, deduced from the analytic-component form (Theorem 1.2.11) of ax-schanuel-power-series; Bakker–Tsimerman §4.1 give an independent o-minimal proof.
acceptance: f = (t, t²) (a parabola, trdeg 1 = rk J): eᵗ and e^{t²} are algebraically independent over ℂ.
This is the functional-transcendence input of the Pila–Zannier proof of the Manin–Mumford statement for (ℂ^×)ⁿ (LogicAndDefinabilityInNumberTheory:LD.6).

sources.match: Verbatim.
The geometric form (as printed; 'coset of a subtorus' is its image under π).

nodes.title: Schanuel's conjecture implies that e and π are algebraically independent
nodes.statement: If SchanuelConjecture holds, then e and π are algebraically independent over ℚ.
hypotheses: Conditional on schanuel-conjecture
proofSteps: 1 and iπ are ℚ-linearly independent (iπ ∉ ℝ); Schanuel gives trdeg ℚ(1, iπ, e, e^{iπ}) = trdeg ℚ(iπ, e) ≥ 2 (Complex.exp_pi_mul_I: e^{iπ} = −1).
i is algebraic, so trdeg ℚ(π, e) = trdeg ℚ(iπ, e) = 2.
acceptance: Unconditionally one knows only that e, π are each transcendental and that π, e^π are algebraically independent (pi-and-exp-pi-algebraically-independent).

sources.match: Verbatim.

nodes.title: Schanuel's conjecture implies the algebraic independence of logarithms
nodes.statement: SchanuelConjecture implies LogarithmsAlgebraicIndependenceConjecture.
hypotheses: Conditional on schanuel-conjecture
proofSteps: Apply Schanuel to z_i = ℓ_i: e^{ℓ_i} are algebraic, so trdeg ℚ(ℓ₁, …, ℓ_n) = trdeg ℚ(ℓ, e^ℓ) ≥ n, i.e. the ℓ_i are algebraically independent.
acceptance: For n = 2 and ℓ = (log 2, log 3) it predicts algebraic independence (open).

nodes.title: The degree capacity of a floored integer grid
nodes.statement: For s ∈ ℕ and B > 0 real, put a = ⌊B⌋ and b = ⌊s/B⌋. Then s < (2a + 1)(b + 1). These are nonnegative integer floors; the result includes s = 0 and 0 < B < 1.
hypotheses: B need not be integral or at least 1.
proofSteps: If B < 1 then a = 0 and B ≤ 2a + 1. If B ≥ 1 then a ≥ 1 and B < a + 1 ≤ 2a + 1.
The floor bound gives s/B < b + 1. Multiplication by B > 0 gives s < B(b + 1) ≤ (2a + 1)(b + 1).
Thus multiplicity b + 1 at 2a + 1 distinct points exceeds degree s. The source's printed factor 2b + 1 is not the degree of its displayed product; see E215.

api.name: DiophantineApproximation.grid_floor_capacity
api.statement: s < (2⌊B⌋+1)(⌊s/B⌋+1) for s ∈ ℕ and B > 0.

acceptance: s = 3, B = 1 gives capacity 12, not the printed 21.
s = 0, B = 1/2 gives capacity 1.

nodes.title: A nonzero univariate jet at a bounded integer point
nodes.statement: Let R be a characteristic-zero integral domain, 0 ≠ P ∈ R[X], natDegree P ≤ s with s ∈ ℕ, and B > 0 real. There exist z ∈ ℤ and i ∈ ℕ with |z| ≤ B, i ≤ s/B and (DⁱP)(z) ≠ 0. Here Dⁱ is Mathlib's univariate Hasse derivative and z is cast into R.
hypotheses: R is a commutative integral domain of characteristic zero, not necessarily a field.
P ≠ 0 and natDegree P ≤ s; equality is not required.
B > 0; the point bound is in ℤ before casting to R.
proofSteps: Set a = ⌊B⌋ and b = ⌊s/B⌋. If the conclusion fails, all Hasse derivatives through order b vanish at every integer from −a to a. Floor bounds put these points and orders within the allowed box.
Multiply by i! to get vanishing of ordinary iterated derivatives through b. Polynomial.lt_rootMultiplicity_iff_isRoot_iterate_derivative gives multiplicity at least b + 1 at each point.

The 2a + 1 integer images are distinct by characteristic zero. Polynomial.count_roots identifies their multiplicities with counts in the root multiset. The disjoint sum of these counts is at least (2a + 1)(b + 1). No comaximality of linear factors over R is asserted.

Polynomial.card_roots' bounds the multiset cardinality by natDegree P ≤ s. Apply grid-floor-capacity for a contradiction. This argument works over domains, so induction needs no rational-function field.

nodes.title: Divided derivatives and partial evaluation of one coordinate
nodes.statement: For a commutative semiring R, P ∈ R[X₀,…,Xₙ], a ∈ R, k ∈ ℕ and residual multi-index d ∈ ℕⁿ, let ev₀,a set X₀ = a and retain the other variables. Then Dᵈ(ev₀,a(D^{k e₀}P)) = ev₀,a(D^{(k,d)}P).
hypotheses: R is a commutative semiring; no characteristic-zero assumption is needed.
Residual variables use Fin n and their original coordinates use Fin.succ.
The full multi-index (k,d) is Finsupp.cons k d.
proofSteps: Expand P as a finite sum of monomials c X₀ʲ X_tail^u. Both sides are additive and R-linear.
For j ≥ k and u ≥ d componentwise, both sides equal c·binom(j,k)·∏ₗbinom(uₗ,dₗ)·a^{j−k}·X_tail^{u−d}. If a derivative order exceeds a corresponding degree, both sides vanish.
First-coordinate and residual derivative supports are disjoint, so the composition binomial factor equals 1. No factorial is introduced.

nodes.title: A bounded partial specialization with nonzero residual polynomial
nodes.statement: Let R be a characteristic-zero integral domain, 0 ≠ P ∈ R[X₀,…,Xₙ], deg_{X₀}P ≤ s and B > 0. There exist z ∈ ℤ and k ∈ ℕ with |z| ≤ B and k ≤ s/B such that Q = ev₀,z(D^{k e₀}P) is nonzero and deg_{Xⱼ}Q ≤ deg_{X_{j+1}}P for every residual coordinate j.
hypotheses: R is a commutative integral domain of characteristic zero; s ∈ ℕ.
P ≠ 0 and B > 0; homogeneity is not required.
The remaining coordinate-degree bounds must survive the choice of point and derivative.
proofSteps: Use MvPolynomial.finSuccEquiv to regard P as f ∈ (R[X₁,…,Xₙ])[X₀]. The algebra equivalence preserves nonzeroness, and natDegree_finSuccEquiv identifies its degree with deg_{X₀}P.

The residual polynomial ring is again a characteristic-zero integral domain. Apply univariate-integer-grid-jet to f, giving z and k with the required bounds and nonzero Polynomial.eval (C z) (Polynomial.hasseDeriv k f).
Use finSuccEquiv_coeff_coeff and the Hasse coefficient formula on monomials to identify this expression with Q = Σ_{j≥k} binom(j,k) z^{j−k} f.coeff j, a finite sum with scalar coefficients.

By degreeOf_coeff_finSuccEquiv each coefficient has residual degrees bounded by those of P. Multiplication by a scalar does not increase a coordinate degree; degreeOf_sum_le supplies the bounds on Q needed for induction.

nodes.title: Non-vanishing of a divided derivative on a rectangular integer grid
nodes.statement: Let R be a characteristic-zero integral domain, 0 ≠ P ∈ R[X₁,…,Xₙ], sⱼ ∈ ℕ with deg_{Xⱼ}P ≤ sⱼ and real Bⱼ > 0. There exist zⱼ ∈ ℤ and a nonnegative multi-index d such that |zⱼ| ≤ Bⱼ and dⱼ ≤ sⱼ/Bⱼ for every j, and DᵈP(z) ≠ 0. Constants and n = 0 are included.
hypotheses: R is a commutative integral domain of characteristic zero; P ≠ 0.
Every coordinate has its own positive real budget and natural degree upper bound.
No homogeneity, positive degree, or bound Bⱼ ≥ 1 is assumed.
proofSteps: Induct on the number of variables. In zero variables P is a nonzero constant; the unique empty point and zero multi-index give nonzero evaluation.
For n+1 variables apply nonzero-partial-grid-specialization to coordinate 0 with s₀ and B₀. It gives z₀, k and nonzero Q with residual degrees bounded by the tail of s.
Apply induction to Q and the tail budgets, obtaining z_tail and d_tail with nonzero residual jet and all tail inequalities.

Use z = (z₀,z_tail) and d = (k,d_tail). partial-specialization-jet followed by tail evaluation identifies the nonzero residual jet with DᵈP(z). The first-coordinate inequalities together with the tail inequalities give all bounds.
Over a characteristic-zero field, multiply by the nonzero product ∏ⱼdⱼ! to recover the ordinary-derivative statement of Evertse's Lemma 25.

nodes.title: Block degrees in a linear substitution
nodes.statement: Let R be a commutative semiring, m,N,r natural numbers, A_h an N-by-r matrix, e an X-multiindex and k a Y-multiindex. Set L_hl(T)=Σ_a A_hla T_ha and c_e,k=[T^k]∏_hl L_hl(T)^e_hl. If c_e,k ≠ 0, then Σ_a k_ha=Σ_l e_hl for every block h.
hypotheses: Zero block counts, zero matrices and r=0 are allowed; no rank or characteristic assumption.
proofSteps: Use the existing weighted-homogeneous predicate with block-indicator weights w_h(h′,a)=1 when h=h′ and 0 otherwise.
Each L_h′l is a sum of scalar multiples of variables of weight w_h(h′,a). The pinned weighted-homogeneous sum, scalar, power and product lemmas give weight Σ_l e_hl for the displayed product.
A nonzero coefficient has that weight by the defining support property. Cancellation can delete coefficients, but cannot introduce a different block degree.

For a fixed k, every e with these equalities satisfies e_hl ≤ Σ_a k_ha; the corresponding finite coordinate box, filtered by the equalities, is exactly E(k). Finsupp's finite interval instance represents this set without introducing a new carrier.
acceptance: Block degree is preserved exactly, not merely bounded above; zero rows impose no exception.

nodes.title: Finite block-linear Hasse chain rule
nodes.statement: For R,m,N,r,A as in block-linear-monomial-support, any F∈R[X], X-multiindex i and Y-multiindex k satisfy D_Y^k((D_X^i F)(AY))=Σ_{e∈E(k)} c_e,k(A) b(i,e) (D_X^{i+e}F)(AY), as polynomials in Y. Here E(k)={e:Σ_l e_hl=Σ_a k_ha for every h}, c_e,k is the coefficient of T^k in ∏_hl(Σ_a A_hla T_ha)^e_hl, and b(i,e)=∏_hl binom(i_hl+e_hl,i_hl).
hypotheses: R is any commutative semiring. No injectivity, nonzero coefficient, homogeneity or positive degree is assumed.
proofSteps: Use the existing multivariate Taylor expansion for H=D^iF, as a polynomial identity: H(AY+AT)=Σ_e (D^eH)(AY)(AT)^e. Obtain this identity over the polynomial coefficient ring by the same monomial binomial expansion; all terms beyond the coordinate degrees vanish by the existing derivative degree bound.

Since A(Y+T)=AY+AT, extract the coefficient of T^k. On the left this is D_Y^k(H(AY)); on the right it is c_e,k(A)(D^eH)(AY). Coefficient extraction and the sum commute because the expansion is finite.
block-linear-monomial-support removes every e outside E(k). Its finite coordinate box also shows that zero summands can be added to obtain precisely the displayed finite sum.
Apply the existing Hasse composition identity, including b(i,e). Natural binomial coefficients are cast into R, so division and characteristic-zero assumptions are unnecessary.
acceptance: The statement is an identity of polynomials, stronger than equality at integer grid points; it includes k=0 and a zero substitution matrix.

Here E(k)={e:Σ_l e_hl=Σ_a k_ha for every h}, c_e,k is the coefficient of T^k in ∏_hl(Σ_a A_hla T_ha)^e_hl, and b(i,e)=∏_hl binom(i_hl+e_hl,i_hl).

nodes.title: A nonzero original jet from a substituted jet
nodes.statement: For R,m,N,r,A,F,i,k as above and y∈R^(mr), if D_Y^k((D_X^iF)(AY))(y)≠0, there is an X-multiindex e with Σ_l e_hl=Σ_a k_ha for each h and (D_X^{i+e}F)(Ay)≠0.
hypotheses: R is any commutative semiring; singular and zero matrices are allowed.
proofSteps: Evaluate block-linear-hasse-chain-rule at y, using the pinned evaluation-composition identity.

A nonzero finite sum has a nonzero summand. If the displayed original jet in that summand were zero, multiplication by its coefficient would make the summand zero. Thus it is nonzero, without a no-zero-divisors assumption.
Membership of the selected exponent in E(k) supplies every exact block-sum identity. This is only a one-way implication: nonzero original jets can cancel after substitution.
acceptance: Do not infer a nonzero composed jet from a chosen nonzero original jet.

nodes.title: Residual block degrees of a nonzero Hasse derivative
nodes.statement: Let R be a commutative semiring and F∈R[X_hl] be block-homogeneous of natural degrees d_h, meaning every exponent μ in its support satisfies Σ_l μ_hl=d_h. If D^jF≠0, then Σ_l j_hl≤d_h for each h, and every exponent ν in the support of D^jF satisfies Σ_l ν_hl=d_h−Σ_l j_hl.
hypotheses: No characteristic or domain hypothesis is needed. The nonzero-derivative hypothesis is required for the order bound.
proofSteps: The existing coefficient formula gives coeff_ν(D^jF)=(∏_hl binom(ν_hl+j_hl,j_hl)) coeff_{ν+j}F.
A nonzero derivative coefficient therefore gives a nonzero coefficient of F at ν+j. Its block sum is d_h; distributing the natural sum gives Σ_l ν_hl+Σ_l j_hl=d_h.

Apply this to every surviving ν for residual homogeneity, and to one surviving ν (which exists by D^jF≠0) for the order bound. Subtract only after this equality; truncating subtraction alone cannot justify the order bound.
acceptance: Use the inherited support condition, equivalently the pinned weighted-homogeneous predicate for each block indicator; no new multihomogeneous structure.

nodes.title: Individual degree after block-linear substitution
nodes.statement: Let R be a commutative semiring, F∈R[X_hl], and d_h∈ℕ. Assume Σ_l μ_hl≤d_h for every μ in the support of F and every h. For any block-linear matrix A_h of size N-by-r, each individual Y_ha-degree of F(AY) is at most d_h.
hypotheses: F may be zero; the block support condition is only an upper bound, not equality. A may have any rank.
proofSteps: Expand F as its finite sum of coefficient monomials using the pinned polynomial support-sum identity.
For a nonzero coefficient of F(AY), some monomial substitution summand has nonzero coefficient. A scalar coefficient cannot turn a zero coefficient into a nonzero one.
Apply block-linear-monomial-support to that summand: its output block sum equals the input block sum, hence is at most d_h. Each individual nonnegative exponent is bounded by that sum.
The pinned degreeOf_le_iff converts the resulting support bound to the individual degree inequality. This proof covers the zero polynomial without extracting a spurious monomial.
acceptance: The needed bound is the whole block degree, not the maximum of the separate input-variable degrees.

nodes.title: A nonzero value at a zero block forces degree zero
nodes.statement: Let R be a commutative semiring and H∈R[X_hl] have block degrees δ_h. If H(x)≠0 and x_h is the zero vector, then δ_h=0.
hypotheses: Block homogeneity means Σ_l μ_hl=δ_h for every exponent μ in the support. Nonzero value is an actual evaluation hypothesis.
proofSteps: If δ_h>0, the block sum of each supported exponent is positive, so some variable of that block occurs to positive power.
All those variables evaluate to zero at x. The pinned eval₂Hom_eq_zero lemma therefore makes every supported monomial vanish and gives H(x)=0, a contradiction.
Natural δ_h must consequently be zero; the argument also covers an empty coordinate block.
acceptance: This is a residual-degree statement, not an inference that the original F has degree zero.

nodes.title: Simultaneous independence of degree-zero blocks
nodes.statement: Let R be a commutative semiring and H∈R[X_hl] have block degrees δ_h. If block vectors x,y agree on every block h with δ_h≠0, then H(x)=H(y). Thus all zero-degree blocks can be replaced simultaneously by arbitrary vectors.
hypotheses: The conclusion is global evaluation independence, not merely constancy at one witness.
proofSteps: For a supported exponent μ, a block with δ_h=0 has a sum of nonnegative exponents equal to zero; every μ_hl in that block is zero.
Every variable appearing in the support of that monomial therefore lies in a nonzero-degree block, where x and y agree.
Apply the pinned evaluation-congruence lemma to conclude equality for H. This establishes simultaneous replacement directly and avoids an unsupported iteration of pointwise independence.
acceptance: Replacing any collection of zero-degree blocks at once preserves the value.

nodes.title: Weighted budget for the extracted grid jet
nodes.statement: Let m≥1,N≥2,d_h>0 be natural numbers and ε>0 real. Put w_d(u)=Σ_h(Σ_l u_hl)/d_h. Let X-multiindices i,e and Y-multiindex k, with N−1 parameters per block, satisfy w_d(i)<mε, Σ_l e_hl=Σ_a k_ha and k_ha≤d_h ε/N. Then w_d(i+e)<(2−1/N)mε<2mε.
hypotheses: All inequalities and divisions are in ℝ; d_h and N are cast before division. No rounding or ε≤1 assumption is needed.
proofSteps: Distribute the finite sums and use positive d_h to obtain w_d(i+e)=w_d(i)+Σ_h(Σ_a k_ha)/d_h.
Sum the N−1 coordinate bounds to get Σ_a k_ha≤(N−1)d_h ε/N. Divide by d_h and sum over m blocks.
Consequently w_d(i+e)≤w_d(i)+m(N−1)ε/N<(2−1/N)mε. Since mε/N>0, this is strictly below 2mε. These are elementary finite-sum and ordered-field calculations, requiring no new index definition.
acceptance: Preserve the initial strict inequality. A nonzero jet only bounds the weighted index weakly by its weight; strictness comes from this budget.

nodes.title: Nonzero block representatives preserving a grid value
nodes.statement: Let K be a field, b_h1,…,b_hr linearly independent vectors of K^N in each of m blocks, choose a₀∈{1,…,r}, and let B≥1. Let H∈K[X_hl] have block degrees δ_h. Suppose z_ha∈ℤ, |z_ha|≤B, and H(x)≠0 for x_h=Σ_a z_ha b_ha. There exist z′_ha∈ℤ with the same bounds such that every x′_h=Σ_a z′_ha b_ha is nonzero and H(x′)=H(x).
hypotheses: r is nonempty, witnessed by a₀. Linear independence suffices; no ambient subspace or spanning assertion is needed. No characteristic-zero assumption is needed for this replacement lemma.
proofSteps: For each block whose x_h is zero, zero-block-forces-degree-zero gives δ_h=0.
Set z′_h=z_h on nonzero blocks, and set z′_h to the integer unit vector at a₀ on zero blocks. Each coefficient remains bounded because B≥1.
LinearIndependent.ne_zero gives b_ha₀≠0, so the new x′_h is nonzero in every replaced block; unreplaced blocks were already nonzero.
On every block with δ_h≠0, x_h was nonzero and is unchanged. zero-degree-block-independence gives H(x′)=H(x) simultaneously.
acceptance: The conclusion is nonzero block vectors, not nonzero individual coordinates. Applied to H=D^jF, obtain its residual block degrees from hasse-residual-block-degrees first.

nodes.title: A nonzero-block grid jet from a nonzero restriction
nodes.statement: Let K be a characteristic-zero field, m≥1,N≥2,d_h positive integers, and 0<ε≤1. Let F∈K[X_hl] have block degrees d_h, and for each h let b_h1,…,b_h,N−1 be linearly independent vectors of K^N. Suppose an X-multiindex i has w_d(i)<mε and the polynomial G(Y)=(D^iF)(Σ_a Y_1a b_1a,…,Σ_a Y_ma b_ma) is nonzero. There exist integers z_ha and an X-multiindex j with |z_ha|≤N/ε, every x_h=Σ_a z_ha b_ha nonzero, w_d(j)<(2−1/N)mε, and (D^jF)(x)≠0.
hypotheses: The nonzero composed polynomial G is an explicit input. F≠0 alone does not suffice. No height or degree-separation assumption is used at this conditional stage.
proofSteps: G≠0 implies D^iF≠0 since polynomial substitution maps zero to zero. hasse-residual-block-degrees gives residual degrees d_h−Σ_l i_hl≤d_h, and block-linear-degree-bound gives the individual parameter-degree bounds for G.

Reindex the m(N−1) variables by finProdFinEquiv and apply rectangular-integer-grid-jet with all budgets N/ε and degree bounds d_h. Transport evaluation, degree and the monomial Hasse coefficient formula back along the finite bijection. The resulting integer y and parameter order k satisfy |y_ha|≤N/ε and k_ha≤d_h ε/N, with a nonzero evaluated Hasse jet.
nonzero-block-linear-jet-extraction gives e with exact block sums and D^{i+e}F(Ay)≠0. Set j=i+e. block-linear-jet-weight-budget gives the strict weight bound.

Apply hasse-residual-block-degrees to the nonzero polynomial H=D^jF. Since N/ε≥1 and N−1≥1, nonzero-block-grid-replacement replaces all zero blocks while preserving the same nonzero Hasse jet and its order.

For the parent theorem, use the existing weighted-index definition to get index≤w_d(j), hence index<2mε. Over characteristic zero, the inherited factorial-to-ordinary derivative API makes this nonvanishing equivalent to the ordinary mixed-derivative form in the parent suggested signature.
acceptance: This closes the purely algebraic and grid portion of Lemma 26 plus the nonzero-block conversion. It does not prove Lemma 24's hyperplane-height nonvanishing or the sharp Roth/Faltings input.

nodes.title: Euclidean height under zero extension
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field, I,J finite types, f:I→J injective, x:I→K nonzero, and y:J→K. If y(f(i))=x(i) and y(j)=0 off the range of f, then H₂(y)=H₂(x). This includes coordinate permutations and relabelling a coefficient support.
proofSteps: At each infinite place the sum of squared embedded coordinates is unchanged: reindex the range by the injection and discard zero coordinates.
At each finite place the maximum is unchanged, since adjoining zero to a nonempty set of nonnegative values cannot change its supremum. The nonzero x ensures that the source index type is nonempty.
Raise the equal local factors to the defining positive exponents and multiply. No change of coefficient field or max-height substitution is involved.

nodes.title: Euclidean height of a nonzero subvector
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field, I,J finite types, f:I→J injective and y:J→K with y∘f nonzero. Then H₂(y∘f)≤H₂(y).
proofSteps: At an infinite place, the subvector sum of squared norms is at most the full sum; at a finite place, its maximum is at most the full maximum. All factors are positive for nonzero vectors.

For each vector the finite-place maximum is 1 outside a finite union of exceptional sets: omit zero coordinates and use NumberField.FinitePlace.hasFiniteMulSupport on the remaining nonzero coordinates. Use one common finite set for both vectors.

Apply monotonicity of positive real powers to each local inequality and multiply the finite products. This is projective subvector monotonicity, not a comparison of arbitrarily rescaled affine coefficient lists.

nodes.title: Projective invariance of Euclidean height
nodes.statement: For a number field K, a finite type I, a nonzero vector x:I→K and a∈K with a≠0, H₂(a·x)=H₂(x).
proofSteps: At an infinite place factor |σ(a)|² out of the squared Euclidean norm. Its contribution after the defining real power is |σ(a)|^{mult/[K:ℚ]}. At a finite place factor |a| out of the maximum, contributing |a|^{1/[K:ℚ]}.
Use the finite-support reduction for the finite products. Their combined scalar factor is the [K:ℚ]-th root of NumberField.prod_abs_eq_one(a), hence 1.

nodes.title: Hyperplane height bounded by binary heights
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field, N≥2, b∈K^N, and p a coordinate with b_p≠0. Then H₂(b)≤∏_{q≠p}H₂((b_p,b_q)).
proofSteps: Normalize c=b/b_p so c_p=1. Scalar invariance gives H₂(c)=H₂(b) and H₂((1,c_q))=H₂((b_p,b_q)).
At an infinite place put t_q=|σ(c_q)|²≥0. The powerset expansion of ∏_{q≠p}(1+t_q) contains the empty-set term 1 and all singleton terms, so 1+Σt_q≤∏(1+t_q). Take the mult/(2[K:ℚ]) power.
At a finite place each max(1,|c_q|)≥1. Their product bounds both 1 and every |c_q|, and hence max_j|c_j|. Raise to 1/[K:ℚ].
Multiply over a common finite set of exceptional places and interchange the finite coordinate products.

nodes.title: A binary direction of large height
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field, N≥2, b∈K^N and b_p≠0. There is q≠p such that H₂(b)≤H₂((b_q,−b_p))^{N−1}. The vector (b_q,−b_p) is nonzero and solves b_p X+b_q Y=0.
proofSteps: Choose q with maximal H₂((b_p,b_q)) among the N−1 other coordinates. This set is nonempty. Each binary height is positive because b_p≠0.
The product bound from height2-normalized-pair-product is at most this maximum to the power N−1. Apply height2-binary-normal-vector.
The second coordinate −b_p is nonzero and b_p b_q+b_q(−b_p)=0. This supplies the point and the height exponent used by sharp Roth.

nodes.title: Coefficient height of a nonzero slice
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field, E,B finite variable types, F∈K[E⊕B], Q=sumAlgEquiv(F)∈(K[B])[E], and e an E-multiindex with Q_e≠0. Then H₂(coefficients of Q_e)≤H₂(coefficients of F).
proofSteps: The native sumAlgEquiv separates the exponent into its E and B restrictions. The coefficient of v in Q_e is exactly the coefficient of F at the combined exponent (e,v). This follows on monomials from the native curry equivalence and extends by finite addition.
Thus the nonzero coefficients of Q_e form a subvector of the coefficients of F, indexed by the injection v↦(e,v). Apply height2-subvector.

nodes.title: Hasse derivatives commute with coefficient slices
nodes.statement: For a commutative semiring R, variable types E,B, F∈R[E⊕B], an E-multiindex e and a B-multiindex i, the e-coefficient of sumAlgEquiv(D^{inr_*i}F) equals D^i((sumAlgEquiv F)_e).
proofSteps: Check the identity on one monomial X_E^u X_B^v: both sides vanish unless u=e, and otherwise equal (∏_b binom(v_b,i_b))X_B^{v−i} with the original coefficient.
Extend by coefficient linearity over the finite support of F. The outer exponents are unchanged; in particular the outer support after differentiation is contained in the original outer support.

nodes.title: A lowest-degree coefficient after an affine substitution
nodes.statement: Let R be a commutative semiring, E,B finite types, Q∈(R[B])[E], e an E-multiindex, x:B→R, and A:B→E→R. Suppose |e|≤|u| for every u∈supp Q, where |u|=Σu_j. Substitute each inner variable X_b by x_b+Σ_j A_bj U_j and each outer variable by U_j. The coefficient of U^e in the resulting polynomial is (Q_e)(x).
proofSteps: Expand Q=Σ_u U^u Q_u(X). In a contribution to exponent e one must have u≤e coordinatewise. The hypothesis |e|≤|u| then forces |u|=|e| and u=e; all proper coordinatewise predecessors have smaller total degree.
For u=e, only the constant coefficient of Q_e(x+A U) contributes. Evaluation at U=0 identifies that constant coefficient with Q_e(x). This also covers Q_e=0 and Q=0.
Use the pinned monomial-product coefficient formula for the first step and eval_eval₂ plus eval_zero for the second. No division, generic-point argument or cancellation assumption is needed.

nodes.title: Residual block degrees of a binary coefficient slice
nodes.statement: Let R be a commutative semiring, m,r natural numbers, E=Fin(m)×Fin(r), B=Fin(m)×Fin(2), and F∈R[E⊕B] with every supported exponent having block-h degree d_h. Put Q=sumAlgEquiv(F). If Q_e≠0, then s_h=Σ_a e_(h,a)≤d_h, and every supported binary exponent v of Q_e satisfies v_(h,0)+v_(h,1)=d_h−s_h.
proofSteps: For each nonzero coefficient (Q_e)_v, combine the outer exponent e with v. Its coefficient in F is the same nonzero scalar. The block degree of that monomial is s_h+v_(h,0)+v_(h,1)=d_h.
A nonzero Q_e has at least one supported v, giving s_h≤d_h. Subtract s_h to obtain the displayed degree for every supported v.

nodes.title: Low-order vanishing passes to a nonzero binary slice
nodes.statement: Let K be an infinite field, E,B finite variable types, F∈K[E⊕B] nonzero, Q=sumAlgEquiv(F), and J any set of B-multiindices. Let x:B→K and A:B→E→K. Suppose for every i∈J and u:E→K, (D^{inr_*i}F)(u,x+A u)=0. Then there is e∈supp Q such that |e| is minimal on supp Q, Q_e≠0, and (D^i Q_e)(x)=0 for every i∈J.
proofSteps: The native algebra equivalence sends F≠0 to Q≠0. Choose e of minimum total degree in the nonempty finite support of Q; Q_e≠0.

For i∈J, differentiate only the inner variables. hasse-derivative-coefficient-slice shows that the resulting outer support is a subset of supp Q, so the same e satisfies the minimum-degree inequality even when its own differentiated coefficient is zero.
Compose the differentiated polynomial with (u,x+A u). It evaluates to zero for every u by hypothesis, hence is the zero polynomial by the pinned infinite-domain polynomial funext theorem.
Its coefficient at e is therefore zero. lowest-degree-affine-coefficient identifies that coefficient with (D^i Q_e)(x). One e works for every i; it is selected from F before differentiation.

Suppose for every i∈J and u:E→K, (D^{inr_*i}F)(u,x+A u)=0. Then there is e∈supp Q such that |e| is minimal on supp Q, Q_e≠0, and (D^i Q_e)(x)=0 for every i∈J.

nodes.title: Restoring the original binary block degrees
nodes.statement: Let R be a nontrivial commutative semiring, m a natural number, P∈R[X_(h,0),X_(h,1)] nonzero of block degrees δ_h, and a_h natural numbers. Put t_(h,0)=a_h and t_(h,1)=0. Then X^t P is nonzero and has block degrees δ_h+a_h.
proofSteps: The coefficient-one monomial translates every supported exponent v to t+v with the same coefficient. It cannot annihilate a nonzero coefficient, even if R has zero divisors.
The translated exponent has block degree a_h+δ_h. Conversely every supported exponent of the product is a translate, by the pinned coefficient formula.

acceptance: The multiplier has coefficient one. Over a ring with zero divisors, an arbitrary nonzero scalar monomial would not give the same nonvanishing conclusion.
